## 1. Introduction and statement of results

Let

$$ d_{k}(n)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}d_{1}\dots d_{k}=n\end{subarray}}1 $$

be the $k$ -fold divisor function, and write $d(n)=d_{2}(n)$ (which we’ll refer to as the divisor function). It is often of interest to estimate sums of the form

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n<X\end{subarray}}a(n)d_{k}(n) $$

for sequences $a:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{C}$ of arithmetic interest. Beyond their own intrinsic interest, questions of estimating (1.1) are relevant to the study of sums over primes

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}p<X\end{subarray}}a(p), $$

which is most clearly seen through an identity of Linnik (see [IK04, Proposition 13.2]) that

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}p^{\nu}<X\end{subarray}}a(p^{\nu})=-\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k\end{subarray}}\frac{(-1)^{k}}{k}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n<X\end{subarray}}a(n)d_{k}^{\prime}(n), $$

where $d_{k}^{\prime}(n)$ is the number of ways to write $n$ as the product of $k$ integers greater than $1$ . Note that $d_{k}^{\prime}$ is closely related to the usual $d_{k}$ for we have

$$ d_{k}^{\prime}(n)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}0\leqslant\ell\leqslant k\end{subarray}}(-1)^{k-\ell}\binom{k}{\ell}d_{\ell}(n), $$

with $d_{0}(n)=\mathbbm{1}_{\begin{subarray}{c}n=1\end{subarray}}$ .

In this paper, we obtain power saving asymptotics for sums of the divisor function along values of a binary quartic form, showing the following result.

#### Theorem 1.

There exists $\delta>0$ such that for $N\geqslant 1$ , we have that

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}m,n\in\mathbb{Z}\\
0<m^{4}+n^{4}\leqslant N\end{subarray}}d(m^{4}+n^{4})=\kappa N^{\frac{1}{2}}(c_{-1}\log N+2(c_{0}-c_{-1}))+O(N^{\frac{1}{2}-\delta}), $$

where

$$ \kappa=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\mathbbm{1}_{x_{1}^{4}+x_{2}^{4}\leqslant 1}\,dx_{1}\,dx_{2}, $$

and $c_{-1},c_{0}$ are such that

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\geqslant 1\end{subarray}}\frac{\rho(q)}{q^{s+1}}=\frac{c_{-1}}{s-1}+c_{0}+O(|s-1|) $$

for $\Re(s)>1$ , where $\rho(q)=\#{\left\{x_{1},x_{2}\in\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}:q|x_{1}^{4}+x_{2}^{4}\right\}}$ .

This improves upon work of Daniel [Dan99], who established asymptotics for (1.5) with a saving in the remainder of $(\log N)^{-1+o(1)}$ . Consequently, the secondary main term was obscured in the prior work, which could not handle the case of two divisors of equal size whose contribution to (1.5) is $\asymp N$ . See §1.1 for further discussion of Daniel’s argument, a sketch of our argument, and a discussion of the relevant bottlenecks.

We do not make $\delta$ explicit (though it is, in principle, computable), since the resulting exponent is almost certainly very poor and does not reflect any substantive barrier. In Theorem 1, the precise value would mainly reflect the sharp cutoff and the loss from sieving out nonsplit primes in our passage to algebraic integers. An explicit exponent is given in Theorem 2, which may be more useful in applications.

We also expect that by combining our results (see Theorem 13.1) with techniques of Hooley, one can show that for any irreducible binary quadratic form $Q$ which does not represent $x^{4}+y^{4}$ and for any $\mathcal{R}\subset\mathbb{R}^{2}\setminus{\left\{0\right\}}$ with $\partial\mathcal{R}$ of finite length, we have

$$ \#{\left\{(x,y)\in X\mathcal{R}:\gcd(x,y)=1,\,\exists u,v\text{ s.t. }Q(u,v)=x^{4}+y^{4}\right\}}\asymp_{\mathcal{R}}\frac{X^{2}}{\sqrt{\log X}}. $$

This answers (with a slightly different quadratic form) a question posed by Loughran in [SBR+24]. The upper bound follows from an upper bound sieve in an argument due to Serre, but the question of a lower bound, as is common with sieving, appears harder. The analogous question (in somewhat more generality) with $x^{4}+y^{4}$ replaced with a binary cubic form is answered by Sofos in [Sof16].

In future work, we intend to generalize Theorem 1 to general binary quartic forms and to replace the divisor function with the Fourier coefficients of general $\GL_{2}$ automorphic forms, thereby obtaining bounds such as (1.8) in greater generality than the example above.

We now state the main theorem, which takes place over $K=\mathbb{Q}(\zeta)$ with $\zeta$ a primitive $8$ th root of unity, and refer the reader to §2 for notation not yet defined.

#### Theorem 2.

Let $M,\Omega\geqslant 1$ and suppose that $\Phi^{\infty}\in C_{c}^{\infty}((K_{\infty}\setminus K_{\infty}^{0})^{2})$ and for $\beta_{1}^{\prime},\beta_{2}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{O}_{K}/M\mathcal{O}_{K}$ , write

$$ \Phi^{f}(\beta_{1},\beta_{2})=\mathbbm{1}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\beta_{1}\equiv\beta_{1}^{\prime}\,(M)\\
\beta_{2}\equiv\beta_{2}^{\prime}\,(M)\end{subarray}}. $$

Suppose furthermore that $\Phi^{\infty}$ satisfies the following properties:

- (1) For all places $v|\infty$ of $K$ and $(x_{1}^{\infty},x_{2}^{\infty})\in\mathrm{supp}(\Phi^{\infty})$ , we have that (1.10)

$$ \frac{1}{\Omega}\ll|x_{1}^{\infty}|_{v},|x_{2}^{\infty}|_{v}\ll\Omega. $$

- (2) For all differential operators $P\in\mathcal{D}(K_{\infty}^{2})$ of order $k$ , we have that (1.11)

$$ \|P\Phi^{\infty}\|_{\infty}\ll_{P}\Omega^{k}. $$

Let $\boldsymbol{\ell}:\mathcal{O}_{K}\to\mathbb{Z}^{2}$ denote the linear map

$$ \boldsymbol{\ell}(n_{0}+n_{1}\zeta+n_{2}\zeta^{2}+n_{3}\zeta^{3})=(n_{3},n_{2}). $$

Then, for any $X_{1},X_{2}\geqslant 1$ , we have that

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}\in\mathcal{O}_{K}\\
\boldsymbol{\ell}(\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2})=0\end{subarray}}\Phi^{\infty}\biggl(\frac{\alpha_{1}}{X_{1}},\frac{\alpha_{2}}{X_{2}}\biggr)\Phi^{f}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2})=X_{1}^{2}X_{2}^{2}\sigma_{\infty}\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\end{subarray}}\sigma_{p}\\
+O\biggl((\Omega M)^{O(1)}X_{1}^{2}X_{2}^{2}\min\biggl((X_{1}X_{2})^{-\eta+o(1)},\frac{X_{1}}{X_{2}}+\frac{1}{X_{1}},\frac{X_{2}}{X_{1}}+\frac{1}{X_{2}}\biggr)\biggr), $$

where

$$ \displaystyle\sigma_{\infty}=\sigma_{\infty}(\Phi^{\infty},\boldsymbol{\ell}) \displaystyle:=\int_{K_{\infty}^{2}}\Phi^{\infty}(x_{1}^{\infty},x_{2}^{\infty})\delta(\boldsymbol{\ell}(x_{1}^{\infty}x_{2}^{\infty}))\,dx_{1}^{\infty}\,dx_{2}^{\infty}, \displaystyle\sigma_{p}=\sigma_{p}(\Phi^{f},\boldsymbol{\ell}) \displaystyle:=\int_{\mathcal{O}_{K,p}^{2}}\Phi^{f}(x_{1}^{p},x_{2}^{p})\delta(\boldsymbol{\ell}(x_{1}^{p}x_{2}^{p}))\,dx_{1}^{p}\,dx_{2}^{p} $$

and

$$ \eta=\frac{1}{236}. $$

### 1.1. Sketch of proof and discussion of argument

We end this section with a discussion of Daniel’s methods in [Dan99], the bottlenecks and limitations in his method, along with a sketch of our proofs of Theorem 1 and Theorem 2. As is typical with such sketches, we will avoid discussing the technicalities of analytic number theory such as smoothing and non-coprimality; we will only discuss the top dyadic ranges which are typically the main difficulty.

Taking the sum in Theorem 1, opening up the divisor function, and splitting the divisors into dyadic intervals, the problem of estimating the left-hand side of (1.5) reduces to estimating

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}d\sim D\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}m,n\sim N^{1/4}\\
d|m^{4}+n^{4}\end{subarray}}1 $$

for $D\ll N^{1/2}$ .

Daniel [Dan99], using lattice point methods of Greaves [Gre71, Gre92], was able to handle divisors of size $D\ll N^{1/2}\log^{-A}N$ . The idea is that the inner sum in (1.17) ought to approximately be

$$ \frac{\rho(d)}{d^{2}}N^{1/2}\approx\frac{N^{1/2}}{D}, $$

which Daniel shows on average for $d\sim D$ , bounding by $O(N^{1/4}\sqrt{D}(\log N)^{O(1)})$ the size of

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}d\sim D\end{subarray}}\biggl|\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n_{1},n_{2}\sim N^{1/4}\\
d|n_{1}^{4}+n_{2}^{4}\end{subarray}}1-\frac{\rho(d)}{d^{2}}N^{1/2}\biggr|. $$

Daniel obtains such a bound by splitting into arithmetic progressions modulo $d$ , interpreting the count over $n_{1},n_{2}$ as an average of lattice point counts, and nontrivially estimating the count on average by using the homogeneity of $x_{1}^{4}+x_{2}^{4}$ to show that the lattices on average do not have a shortest vector of size smaller than one would expect given the covolume.

We remark that Friedlander–Iwaniec in [FI10, Theorem 22.20] obtain the same level of distribution of $1/2$ as Daniel with Poisson summation, in which case the homogeneity plays a related role, this time providing more cancellation in the resulting exponential sums than one would expect for an inhomogeneous polynomial.

The large moduli are treated similarly, but at this point, there is a strict limit to the saving one can obtain. Focusing on the case of $D\asymp N^{1/2}$ , the inner sum in (1.17) has $1$ term on average and so one cannot hope for a bound on (1.19) better than $N^{1/2}$ , and indeed, this is the bound Daniel obtains. Summing over the $\log\log N$ scales $N^{1/2}\log^{-A}N\ll D\ll N^{1/2}$ , this gives Daniel an asymptotic for (1.5) with remainder term $O(N^{1/2}\log\log N)$ .

To obtain anything more than a saving of $(\log N)^{1-o(1)}$ over the main term, it is necessary then to obtain estimates for the sum (1.19) without the absolute values. This is the barrier we refer to as the limit of the hyperbola method: the point at which the sequence is too sparse to allow for further gains without exploiting cancellation in more than one divisor.

One direct way to seek to breach this barrier, following either Daniel’s or Friedlander–Iwaniec’s treatment, is to seek equidistribution of roots of the congruence $x_{1}^{4}+x_{2}^{4}\equiv 0(q)$ as $q$ varies (beyond the equidistribution already implied by the homogeneity). Such equidistribution of roots of a polynomial congruence to a varying modulus is a notoriously difficult problem. This is only known for irreducible single variable quadratic polynomials.

Incidentally, the case of single variable quadratic polynomials is the only case of the hyperbola method barrier having been breached, which was first done by Hooley [Hoo63] who obtained power saving asymptotics for sums of $d(n^{2}+a)$ . Every aspect of the single variable case turns out to be intimately tied to $\GL_{2}$ automorphic forms (see [Sar84, TT13], for example), but no such interpretation appears to exist for any other natural case of either polynomial root equidistribution or for the divisor sum problem (though see [Wel22]).

Our work represents the first case of this hyperbola method barrier being breached for polynomial sequences since Hooley [Hoo63]. We shall now sketch our argument. As is typical with such sketches, the symbol “=” should not be interpreted too literally for it shall hide many nongeneric ranges and phenomena we deal with carefully in the full proof.

We proceed with the estimation of the sum

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}d\sim N^{1/2}\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}m,n\sim N^{1/4}\\
d|m^{4}+n^{4}\end{subarray}}1=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}a_{1}a_{2}=m^{4}+n^{4}\\
a_{1},a_{2}\sim X^{2}\\
m,n\sim X\end{subarray}}1 $$

“as a whole”, treating $a_{1},a_{2}$ equally (we’ve relabelled $X\asymp N^{1/4}$ for future compatibility with Theorem 2). Passing to the number field $K=\mathbb{Q}(\zeta)$ , we observe that $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(m+n\zeta)=m^{4}+n^{4}$ , and therefore, by unique factorization11 1 Finiteness of the class group would suffice in practice, there is (modulo minor technicalities on split primes22 2 In the case at hand, this holds as stated so long as $(m,n)=1$ ) a bijection between factorizations into rational integers $m^{4}+n^{4}=a_{1}a_{2}$ and factorizations $(m+n\zeta)=\mathfrak{a}_{1}\mathfrak{a}_{2}$ into integral ideals $\mathfrak{a}_{1},\mathfrak{a}_{2}\subset\mathcal{O}_{K}$ , with $\mathfrak{a}_{i}\mapsto N\mathfrak{a}_{i}=a_{i}$ giving one direction of the correspondence.

Writing $\mathfrak{a}_{i}=(\alpha_{i})$ for some $\alpha_{i}\in\mathcal{O}_{K}$ by picking some fundamental domain for $\mathcal{O}_{K}/\mathcal{O}_{K}^{\times}$ and summing over the $\alpha_{i}$ , detecting if $\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}$ is of the form $m+n\zeta$ , we obtain that

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}a_{1}a_{2}=m^{4}+n^{4}\\
a_{1},a_{2}\sim X^{2}\\
m,n\sim X\end{subarray}}1=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}\sim X^{1/2}\end{subarray}}\mathbbm{1}_{\boldsymbol{\ell}(\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2})=0}. $$

The estimation of the right-hand side of the above is the content of Theorem 2, whose proof we now sketch.

We detect the condition $\boldsymbol{\ell}(\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2})=0$ with a perturbation of a two dimensional delta method due to [LMV24], the statement of which amounts to

$$ \mathbbm{1}_{\boldsymbol{\ell}(\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2})=0}\approx-\frac{L^{2}}{X^{2/3}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\sim X^{2/3}L\end{subarray}}\mathbbm{1}_{q|\boldsymbol{\ell}(\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2})}+\frac{L^{2}}{X^{2/3}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}d\ll X^{1/3}/L\\
\mathbf{c}\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}\\
|\mathbf{c}|d\sim X^{1/3}/L\\
(c_{1},c_{2})=1\end{subarray}}\frac{dL^{1/2}}{X^{2/3}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\sim X^{2/3}/(dL^{1/2})\end{subarray}}\mathbbm{1}_{\begin{subarray}{c}dq|\det(\mathbf{c},\boldsymbol{\ell}(\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}))\\
d|\boldsymbol{\ell}(\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2})\end{subarray}}, $$

where $L$ is a small power of $X$ to be chosen (note here that $|\boldsymbol{\ell}(\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2})|\ll X$ ). Note that the conductor of the conditions on the first sum is $\ll X^{2/3}L$ and on the second $\ll X^{2/3}/L^{1/2}$ ; the purpose of the introduction of the parameter $L$ is to shift difficulty from the second sum onto the first sum for reasons that will soon be clear.

After applying Poisson summation in $\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}$ , we are reduced to bounding, in the generic case (so apart from main terms coming from zero frequencies)

$$ \Sigma_{1}=\frac{1}{L^{3}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\sim X^{2/3}L\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}\sim X^{1/6}L\end{subarray}}S_{1}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2};q), $$

where

$$ S_{1}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2};q)=\frac{1}{q^{3}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\beta_{1},\beta_{2}\in\mathcal{O}_{K}/(q)\\
\boldsymbol{\ell}(\beta_{1}\beta_{2})\equiv 0\,(q)\end{subarray}}e_{q}\biggl(\Tr\frac{\alpha_{1}\beta_{1}+\alpha_{2}\beta_{2}}{\delta_{K}}\biggr) $$

turns out to be multiplicative in $q$ and satisfy

$$ S_{1}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2};p)=-1+\#{\left\{x\,(p):n_{0}+\dots+n_{3}x^{3}\equiv 0\,(p)\right\}}+O\biggl(\frac{1}{p}\biggr) $$

with the notation $\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}=n_{0}+\dots+n_{3}\zeta^{3}$ from now on, and

$$ \Sigma_{2}=X^{2/3}L^{5/2}\frac{L^{2}}{X^{2/3}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}|\mathbf{c}|d\sim X^{1/3}/L\\
(c_{1},c_{2})=1\end{subarray}}\frac{dL^{1/2}}{X^{2/3}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\sim X^{2/3}/(dL^{1/2})\end{subarray}}\\
\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}\sim X^{1/6}/L^{1/2}\end{subarray}}S_{1}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2};d)\mathbbm{1}_{q|n_{0}c_{1}^{3}-n_{1}c_{1}^{2}c_{2}+n_{2}c_{1}c_{2}^{2}-n_{3}c_{2}^{3}}. $$

At this point, we wish to bound $\max(|\Sigma_{1}|,|\Sigma_{2}|)$ , and the trivial bounds (bounding each term by $X^{o(1)}$ on average) on $\Sigma_{1},\Sigma_{2}$ are $X^{2}L^{6},X^{2}L^{-3/2}$ , respectively, so when $L=1$ , we are right at the boundary.

We are able to go beyond the trivial bound for $\Sigma_{1}$ by noting that because of (1.24), we have that

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\end{subarray}}\frac{S_{1}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2};q)}{q^{s}}\approx\frac{L_{k_{\alpha}}(s)}{\zeta(s)}=L(s,\pi_{\alpha}), $$

where $k_{\alpha}$ is the splitting field over $\mathbb{Q}$ of $f_{\alpha}(x)=n_{0}+\dots+n_{3}x^{3}$ , and $\pi_{\alpha}$ is a $\GL_{2}$ cusp form of level $n_{3}^{2}\mathrm{Disc}(n_{0}+\dots+n_{3}\zeta^{3})\ll X^{2}L^{4}$ . Letting $(\lambda_{\alpha}(n))_{n\geqslant 1}$ be the Fourier coefficients, we are at this point reduced to bounding

$$ \frac{1}{L^{3}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha\sim X^{1/3}L^{2}\end{subarray}}\biggl|\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\sim X^{2/3}L\end{subarray}}\lambda_{\alpha}(q)\biggr|. $$

At this point, we will use very little about $\lambda_{\alpha}$ to proceed. Using Hölder’s inequality and the multiplicativity of $\lambda_{\alpha}$ , at the cost of introducing coefficients, we can lengthen the sum over $q$ and reduce ourselves to obtaining a power saving over the trivial bound for

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha\sim X^{1/3}L^{2}\end{subarray}}\biggl(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\sim X^{2/3}L\end{subarray}}\lambda_{\alpha}(q)\biggr)^{8}\approx\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha\sim X^{1/6}L\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\sim X^{16/3}L^{8}\end{subarray}}d_{8}(q)\lambda_{\alpha}(q). $$

Now, applying Cauchy to smooth out the $d_{8}(q)$ , we are reduced to getting a power saving over the trivial bound for

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha,\alpha^{\prime}\sim X^{1/3}L^{2}\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\sim X^{16/3}L^{7}\end{subarray}}\lambda_{\alpha}(q)\lambda_{\alpha^{\prime}}(q). $$

Note that at this point, the inner sum is essentially over the coefficients of the Rankin-Selberg convolution, whose L-function $L(s,\pi_{\alpha}\times\pi_{\alpha^{\prime}})$ has conductor $\ll(X^{2}L^{4})^{4}=X^{8}L^{16}$ . It is known that $\zeta_{k_{\alpha},p}\neq\zeta_{k_{\alpha^{\prime}},p}$ for infinitely many primes $p$ whenever $k_{\alpha}\neq k_{\alpha^{\prime}}$ , and so it follows that $L(s,\pi_{\alpha}\times\pi_{\alpha^{\prime}})$ has no pole at $s=1$ . A convexity bound (equivalently, one application of Voronoi summation followed by a trivial bound) yields that we may save $X^{-4/3}L^{O(1)}$ over the trivial bound on the inner sum whenever $k_{\alpha}\neq k_{\alpha^{\prime}}$ . A crude count (ranging over the constant term) yields that $k_{\alpha}=k_{\alpha^{\prime}}$ a $O(X^{-1/3}L^{-2})$ -fraction of the time, and therefore, $\Sigma_{1}\ll X^{2-\delta}L^{O(1)}$ for some $\delta>0$ .

Putting this together with the bound $|\Sigma_{2}|\ll X^{2}L^{-3/2}$ and taking $L$ a sufficiently small power of $X$ depending on $\delta$ , we obtain that $|\Sigma_{1}|+|\Sigma_{2}|\ll X^{2-\eta}$ for some $\eta>0$ , as desired.

We end this section with some remarks on what more our methods should yield, in principle. With some work handling the class group, it should be possible to prove Theorem 1 with $m^{4}+n^{4}$ replaced by any irreducible binary quartic form.

Furthermore, note that at no point in our proof did we truly use the convolution structure of the divisor function: all we do is Poisson in both variables simultaneously. Therefore, we expect that Theorem 1 should also hold with $d(n)$ replaced by the Fourier coefficients of any $\GL_{2}$ automorphic form (perhaps assuming Ramanujan), with the substitute for unique factorization functoriality of the base change lift to the splitting field of the binary quartic. The presence of a main term should then depend on the cuspidality of the automorphic form after lifting.

## 2. Notation

Fix $\delta_{K}=4\zeta^{3}$ as a generator of the different ideal, and for $\alpha,\beta\in K$ set

$$ \langle\alpha,\beta\rangle:=\Tr\biggl(\frac{\alpha\beta}{\delta_{K}}\biggr), $$

the trace pairing. Note that $\alpha=x_{0}+x_{1}\zeta+x_{2}\zeta^{2}+x_{3}\zeta^{3}\in K$ satisfies $\langle\alpha,1\rangle=x_{3}$ . We write $\psi(\alpha)=e(\langle\alpha,1\rangle)$ and let $\psi_{\gamma}(\alpha)=\psi(\alpha/\gamma)$ .

Let $K_{\infty}=K\otimes_{\mathbb{Q}}\mathbb{R}$ , $K_{p}=K\otimes_{\mathbb{Q}}\mathbb{Q}_{p}$ , and $\mathcal{O}_{K,p}=\mathcal{O}_{K}\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}\mathbb{Z}_{p}$ . The measure we take on $K_{\infty}$ and $K_{p}$ will be the Haar measure, normalized so that $\vol(\mathcal{O}_{K,p})=1$ . The norm can be extended as a function from $K_{\infty}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geqslant 0}$ and $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ can be extended to $K_{\infty},K_{p}$ as well.

We let $|-|_{\infty}$ and $|-|_{p}$ be defined on $K_{\infty}$ and $K_{p}$ as

$$ \displaystyle|x|_{\infty}:=\biggl(\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}v|\infty\end{subarray}}|x_{v}|_{v}\biggr)^{1/[K:\mathbb{Q}]}\quad\text{ and }\quad|x|_{p}:=\biggl(\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}v|p\end{subarray}}|x_{v}|_{v}\biggr)^{1/[K:\mathbb{Q}]}. $$

On $K$ , we have that $|x|_{\infty}=|N(x)|^{1/[K:\mathbb{Q}]}$ and similarly at $p$ . With this, we write $K_{\infty}^{0}={\left\{x\in K_{\infty}:|x|_{\infty}=0\right\}}$ .

We also write $|x|_{\sup}=\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}v|\infty\end{subarray}}|\sigma_{v}(x)|$ . Clearly, we have $|x|_{\infty}\leqslant|x|_{\sup}$ .

For a vector $\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},x_{2})$ , we write $|\mathbf{x}|=\sqrt{x_{1}^{2}+x_{2}^{2}}$ and call a vector $\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},x_{2})\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}$ primitive if $(x_{1},x_{2})=1$ . Define $\mathbf{x}^{\perp}:=(-x_{2},x_{1})$ .

For the rest of the paper, Greek letters such as $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ will generally denote elements of $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ unless otherwise specified. $\delta$ in particular will generally denote a sufficiently small fixed positive quantity, and may vary between different occurrences.

For a positive integer $q$ , we employ the standard notation $\displaystyle\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}a\,(q)\end{subarray}}$ and $\displaystyle\mathop{\mathop{\sideset{}{{}^{*}}{\sum}}}_{a\,(q)}$ to denote sums over residue classes modulo $q$ and primitive residue classes modulo $q$ respectively. On the other hand, $\displaystyle\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha\,(q)\end{subarray}}$ with greek letters refers to a sum $\displaystyle\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha\in\mathcal{O}_{K}/q\mathcal{O}_{K}\end{subarray}}$ . Bold letters such as $\mathbf{c}$ denote vectors in $\mathbb{Z}^{2}$ , with components denoted with subscripts of the corresponding non-bold letter (e.g. $\mathbf{c}=(c_{1},c_{2})$ ).

Throughout, implied constants may depend on $\Omega^{O(1)}$ ; we do not mention this dependence further. For instance, we may say that for $(x_{1}^{\infty},x_{2}^{\infty})$ in the support of $\Phi^{\infty}$ , by the condition (1.10), we have

$$ |x_{j}^{\infty}|_{\infty}\asymp|x_{j}^{\infty}|_{\sup}. $$

On the other hand, the statement $\exp(\Omega)\ll 1$ does not comply with our convention here.

## 3. Preliminary lemmas

### 3.1. Polynomial root counts in residue classes

We shall need the following lemma on counting roots of polynomials modulo prime powers.

#### Lemma 3.1.

Suppose that $f(X)\in\mathbb{Z}[X]$ has degree $3$ and $p$ is prime such that $p\nmid f(X)$ . Then, for all $k\geqslant 0$ we have

$$ \#{\{x(p^{k}):f(x)\equiv 0(p^{k})\}}\ll(k+1)^{k-1}(p^{k},\mathrm{Disc}(f))^{2/3}. $$

#### Proof.

This follows when $p^{k}|\mathrm{Disc}(f)$ from a result of Kamke [Kam24, (35)] which provides a bound of $\leqslant(k+1)^{k-1}p^{2k/3}$ for the count in question, and otherwise, follows from work of Sándor [S52], who showed a bound of $\leqslant np^{v_{p}(\mathrm{Disc}(f))/2}$ when $v_{p}(\mathrm{Disc}(f))<k$ . ∎

### 3.2. Factorization in a rank $2$ submodule of $\mathcal{O}_{K}$

In this subsection, we shall prove some basic facts about the factorization of elements in the orthogonal complement of $\boldsymbol{\ell}(\mathcal{O}_{K})$ in $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ , given by $\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}\zeta$ .

#### Lemma 3.2.

Take $p$ a rational prime, $x,y\in\mathbb{Z}$ , and $\mathfrak{p}_{1},\mathfrak{p}_{2}|p$ prime ideals in $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ such that $\mathfrak{p}_{1},\mathfrak{p}_{2}|x+y\zeta$ . Then, at least one of the following holds:

- (1) $p|x,y$ .

- (2) $\mathfrak{p}_{1}=\mathfrak{p}_{2}$ , $N\mathfrak{p}_{1}=p$ .

In particular, if $p\nmid(x,y)$ , we have

$$ p^{m}|N(x+y\zeta)\iff\text{ there exists }\,\mathfrak{p}|p\,\text{ such that }\,N\mathfrak{p}=p\text{ and }\mathfrak{p}^{m}|x+y\zeta. $$

#### Proof.

Suppose now that $p\nmid(x,y)$ . Without loss of generality, suppose that $p\nmid y$ , which we can harmlessly scale to be $1$ .

The condition that $\mathfrak{p}_{1},\mathfrak{p}_{2}|x+\zeta$ implies that $I=(p,x+\zeta)\subset\mathfrak{p}_{1},\mathfrak{p}_{2}$ . Then, we have that $\mathcal{O}_{K}/I$ is isomorphic to

$$ (\mathcal{O}_{K}/p\mathcal{O}_{K})/(x+\zeta)\cong\mathbb{Z}[\zeta]/(p,x+\zeta)\cong\mathbb{Z}[T]/(p,T^{4}+1,T+x)\cong(\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})/(x^{4}+1). $$

It follows that $N(I)=p$ and that $\mathfrak{p}_{1}=\mathfrak{p}_{2}=I$ , from which the desired result follows. ∎

#### Lemma 3.3.

For $p$ a rational prime and $k\geqslant 1$ , we have that

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}x(p^{k})\end{subarray}}N((x+\zeta,p^{k}))\ll p^{k}. $$

#### Proof.

This follows by noting that for $k\geqslant 1$ , Lemma 3.2 implies that $N((x+\zeta,p^{k}))=(x^{4}+1,p^{k})$ , at which point the desired result follows from Hensel’s lemma. ∎

### 3.3. Poisson summation over $K$

The statement of Poisson summation we shall use is the following.

#### Proposition 3.4.

Suppose that $w\in\mathcal{S}(K_{\infty})$ . Then, for any $\gamma\in\mathcal{O}_{K}\setminus{\left\{0\right\}}$ , $g_{\gamma}:\mathcal{O}_{K}/(\gamma)\to\mathbb{C}$ and $X>0$ , we have that

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha\in\mathcal{O}_{K}\end{subarray}}g_{\gamma}(\alpha)w\biggl(\frac{\alpha}{X}\biggr)=\frac{X^{4}}{\sqrt{N(\gamma)}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha\in\mathcal{O}_{K}\end{subarray}}\hat{g}_{\gamma}(\alpha)\hat{w}\biggl(\frac{\alpha X}{\gamma}\biggr) $$

where the transforms $\hat{w},\hat{g}_{\gamma}$ are defined as

$$ \hat{w}(y)=\int_{K_{\infty}}w(x^{\infty})e(-\langle x^{\infty},y\rangle)\,dx^{\infty}, $$

$$ \hat{g}_{\gamma}(\alpha)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N(\gamma)}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\beta\in\mathcal{O}_{K}/(\gamma)\end{subarray}}g_{\gamma}(\beta)\psi_{\gamma}(\alpha\beta). $$

Note that this simply amounts to Poisson summation for sums over a sublattice of $\mathbb{Z}^{4}$ with coordinates $n_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}$ such that $\alpha=n_{0}+\dots+n_{3}\zeta^{3}$ . In the case we are concerned with, we will only ever be considering $\gamma\in\mathbb{Z}$ , so the correspondence is even more plain.

We elect to work over $K$ rather than return to sums over $\mathbb{Z}^{8}$ because doing so motivates maneuvers in our exponential sum evaluation which might have otherwise been opaque.

### 3.4. Factorization and coefficients of cubic Dedekind zeta functions

We record in this subsection some facts about cubic Dedekind zeta functions that will be used later. The setup we will suppose throughout is that for some $n_{0},\dots,n_{3}\in\mathbb{Z}$ , $f(x)=n_{3}x^{3}+\dots+n_{0}$ , and let $k=\mathbb{Q}[x]/(f(x))$ be a cubic extension in which $f$ has a root. With $k^{\mathrm{cl}}/\mathbb{Q}$ the Galois closure of $k/\mathbb{Q}$ , we’ll suppose that $\Gal(k^{\mathrm{cl}}/\mathbb{Q})\cong S_{3}$ .

Then, we have the following lemma:

#### Lemma 3.5.

We have that the degree $3$ Dedekind zeta function $\zeta_{k}(s)$ factors as $\zeta(s)L(s,\pi)$ , where $\pi$ is a dihedral cuspidal automorphic representations over $\mathbb{Q}$ of level $N|n_{3}^{2}\mathrm{Disc}(f)$ and central character $\omega_{\pi}=\chi_{L}$ .

In particular,

$$ L(s,\pi)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n\end{subarray}}\frac{\lambda_{\pi}(n)}{n^{s}} $$

with $|\lambda_{\pi}(n)|\leqslant d(n)$ and satisfies

$$ \lambda_{\pi}(p)=-1+\#{\left\{x\in\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}:f(x)\equiv 0\,(p)\right\}} $$

for $p\nmid N$ .

#### Proof.

Let $G=\Gal(k^{\mathrm{cl}}/\mathbb{Q})\cong S_{3}$ , $H=\Gal(k^{\mathrm{cl}}/k)$ . Also, let $L$ be the unique quadratic subfield of $k^{\mathrm{cl}}$ (the fixed field of $A_{3}$ ). Furthermore, let $\Delta_{k}$ be the discriminant of $k/\mathbb{Q}$ .

Then, we have that $\zeta_{k}(s)=\zeta(s)L_{L}(s,\psi)$ for $\psi$ an order $3$ Dirichlet character of conductor $\mathfrak{f}$ such that $N\mathfrak{f}|\Delta_{k}$ . The existence of $\pi$ of level dividing $\Delta_{k}$ with $L(s,\pi)=L_{L}(s,\psi)$ is standard.

It remains to show that $\Delta_{k}|n_{3}^{2}\mathrm{Disc}(f)$ .

To see this, note that $k=\mathbb{Q}[x]/(f_{0}(x))$ for $f_{0}(x)=n_{3}^{2}f(x/n_{3})$ monic. Then, we have that because $f_{0}$ is monic, $\mathrm{Disc}_{k}|\mathrm{Disc}(f_{0})$ , so the desired result follows upon noting that $\mathrm{Disc}(f_{0}(x))=n_{3}^{2}\mathrm{Disc}(f)$ , from which the desired result follows. ∎

We record the following consequence of Rankin-Selberg too.

#### Proposition 3.6.

Suppose that $f_{1},f_{2}\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ are of degree $3$ with $\Gal(f_{i})\cong S_{3}$ , and suppose furthermore that $k_{1}\not\simeq k_{2}$ , with $k_{i}=\mathbb{Q}[x]/(f_{i}(x))$ . Let $\pi_{i}$ be the corresponding automorphic representations from Lemma 3.5. Then, we have that for any $\phi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}_{>0})$ with $|\phi|\leqslant\mathbbm{1}_{[1,2]}$ and $B\geqslant 1$ , we have that

$$ \mathop{\mathop{\sideset{}{{}^{\flat}}{\sum}}}_{(q,B)=1}\lambda_{\pi_{1}}(q)\lambda_{\pi_{2}}(q)\phi\biggl(\frac{q}{Q}\biggr)\ll Q^{\frac{1}{2}+o(1)}(N_{1}N_{2})^{\frac{1}{2}+o(1)}B^{o(1)}\|\phi^{\prime\prime\prime}\|_{\infty}. $$

#### Proof.

We begin by noting that for $\Re s>1$ ,

$$ L(s):=\mathop{\mathop{\sideset{}{{}^{\flat}}{\sum}}}_{(q,B)=1}\frac{\lambda_{\pi_{1}}(q)\lambda_{\pi_{2}}(q)}{q^{s}}=\frac{L(s,\pi_{1}\times\pi_{2})}{L(2s,\omega_{\pi_{1}}\omega_{\pi_{2}})}\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\end{subarray}}\biggl(1+\frac{\mathbbm{1}_{p|B}}{p^{s}}+\frac{O(1)}{p^{2s}}\biggr). $$

As long as $\pi_{1,p}$ is not equal to $\pi_{2,p}$ at all but finitely many primes, $L(s,\pi_{1}\times\pi_{2})$ is holomorphic. Since $k_{1}\not\simeq k_{2}$ and $\zeta_{k_{i}}(s)=\zeta(s)L(s,\pi_{i})$ , it follows from a result of Perlis [Per77] and Perlis and Stuart [SP95] that for infinitely many primes, $\pi_{1,p}\not\simeq\pi_{2,p}$ . In particular, in our situation, we may conclude that $L(s)$ has an analytic continuation to $\Re s>1/2$ .

Therefore, by Mellin inversion, moving the contour to the $1/2+1/\log X$ -line, we have that

$$ \mathop{\mathop{\sideset{}{{}^{\flat}}{\sum}}}_{(q,B)=1}\lambda_{\pi_{1}}(q)\lambda_{\pi_{2}}(q)\phi\biggl(\frac{q}{Q}\biggr)=\int_{(2)}L(s)Q^{s}\tilde{\phi}(s)\,ds\\
\ll(BN_{1}N_{2})^{o(1)}Q^{\frac{1}{2}+o(1)}\|\phi^{\prime\prime\prime}\|_{\infty}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\biggl|L\biggl(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{\log X}+it,\pi_{1}\times\pi_{2}\biggr)\biggr|\frac{\,dt}{1+|t|^{3}}. $$

Here we have integrated by parts three times on $\tilde{\phi}(s)=\int_{0}^{\infty}\phi(x)x^{s-1}dx$ . The desired result follows immediately from the convexity bound $L(s,\pi_{1}\times\pi_{2})\ll((1+|s|)^{4}(N_{1}N_{2})^{2})^{1/4+o(1)}$ . ∎

## 4. The two dimensional $\delta$ -method

In this section, we show the expansion of the two dimensional $\delta$ -symbol we require. We follow along the lines of [LMV24], though we shall not require expanding into additive characters, the lack thereof simplifies the proof.

Furthermore, a perturbation of the parameters in [LMV24] is required, so we need to show the following version of their result ourselves.

#### Theorem 4.1.

Suppose that $\mathbf{n}\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}$ with $|n_{1}|,|n_{2}|<X$ . Take $1\ll D\ll X^{1/2}$ . Let $\omega_{1}\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}_{>0})$ . Let $\omega_{2}\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R})$ be even with $\omega_{2}(0)=0$ . Further suppose that

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\omega_{1}(|\mathbf{x}|)\,d\mathbf{x}=\int_{\mathbb{R}_{>0}}\omega_{2}(x)\,dx=1. $$

Then, for any $A>0$ , we have that

$$ \mathbbm{1}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{n}=0\end{subarray}}=\frac{1}{D^{2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}d\geqslant 1\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{c}\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}\\
(c_{1},c_{2})=1\end{subarray}}\omega_{1}\biggl(\frac{|\mathbf{c}|d}{D}\biggr)\frac{d}{\sqrt{DX}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\geqslant 1\end{subarray}}\biggl(\omega_{2}\biggl(\frac{dq}{\sqrt{DX}}\biggr)-\omega_{2}\biggl(\frac{\det(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{n})}{q\sqrt{DX}}\biggr)\biggr)\mathbbm{1}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\begin{subarray}{c}\det(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{n})\equiv 0\,(dq)\\
\mathbf{n}\equiv 0\,(d)\end{subarray}\end{subarray}}\\
-\frac{2}{D^{2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\geqslant 1\end{subarray}}\omega_{1}\biggl(\frac{|\mathbf{n}|}{qD}\biggr)\mathbbm{1}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{n}\equiv 0\,(q)\end{subarray}}+O_{A,\omega_{1},\omega_{2}}(D^{-A}), $$

As an ingredient to the proof of Theorem 4.1, we shall require the following simple version of the usual $\delta$ -method of Duke–Friedlander–Iwaniec [DFI93].

#### Proposition 4.2.

Suppose that $\omega\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R})$ is even with $\omega(0)=0$ and $\hat{\omega}(0)=2$ . Then, for any $A>0$ , $Q\geqslant 1$ , and $n\in\mathbb{Z}$ , we have that

$$ \mathbbm{1}_{\begin{subarray}{c}n=0\end{subarray}}=\frac{1}{Q}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\geqslant 1\end{subarray}}\biggl(\omega\biggl(\frac{q}{Q}\biggr)-\omega\biggl(\frac{n}{qQ}\biggr)\biggr)\mathbbm{1}_{\begin{subarray}{c}n\equiv 0\,(q)\end{subarray}}+O_{A,\omega}(Q^{-A}). $$

#### Proof of Theorem 4.1.

We begin by noting for all $\mathbf{n}\neq 0$ , there is an involution of

$$ {\left\{(\mathbf{c},d,q):n=\mathbf{c}dq,\mathbf{c}\text{ primitive},d,q\geqslant 1\right\}} $$

given by $(\mathbf{c},d,q)\mapsto(\mathbf{c},q,d)$ . Therefore, for $\mathbf{n}\neq 0$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle 0= \displaystyle\ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{c}\text{ primitive}\\
\langle\mathbf{c},\mathbf{n}\rangle>0\end{subarray}}\mathbbm{1}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\det(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{n})=0\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}dq\mathbf{c}=\mathbf{n}\end{subarray}}\biggl(\omega_{1}\biggl(\frac{|\mathbf{c}|d}{D}\biggr)-\omega_{1}\biggl(\frac{|\mathbf{n}|}{qD}\biggr)\biggr) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{c}\text{ primitive}\\
\langle\mathbf{c},\mathbf{n}\rangle>0\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}d|\mathbf{n}\end{subarray}}\mathbbm{1}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\det(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{n}/d)=0\end{subarray}}\,\omega_{1}\biggl(\frac{|\mathbf{c}|d}{D}\biggr)-\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q|\mathbf{n}\end{subarray}}\omega_{1}\biggl(\frac{|\mathbf{n}|}{qD}\biggr) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\ \frac{1}{2}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{c}\text{ primitive}\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}d|\mathbf{n}\end{subarray}}\mathbbm{1}_{\det(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{n}/d)=0}\,\omega_{1}\biggl(\frac{|\mathbf{c}|d}{D}\biggr)-\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q|\mathbf{n}\end{subarray}}\omega_{1}\biggl(\frac{|\mathbf{n}|}{qD}\biggr). $$

At this point, we apply Theorem 4.2 with $Q=\sqrt{DX}/d,\omega=\omega_{2}$ to expand out $\mathbbm{1}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\det(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{n}/d)=0\end{subarray}}$ and obtain that (4.5) equals

$$ 0=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}d|\mathbf{n}\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{c}\text{ primitive}\end{subarray}}\omega_{1}\biggl(\frac{|\mathbf{c}|d}{D}\biggr)\frac{1}{Q}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\geqslant 1\end{subarray}}\biggl(\omega_{2}\biggl(\frac{q}{Q}\biggr)-\omega_{2}\biggl(\frac{\det(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{n}/d)}{qQ}\biggr)\biggr)\mathbbm{1}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\det(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{n}/d)\equiv 0\,(q)\end{subarray}}\\
-\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\geqslant 1\end{subarray}}\mathbbm{1}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{n}\equiv 0\,(q)\end{subarray}}\,\omega_{1}\biggl(\frac{|\mathbf{n}|}{qD}\biggr)+O(D^{-A}) $$

for any $A>0$ . Here we use that $d\ll D\ll X^{1/2}$ to obtain the error term $O(D^{-A})$ . This completes the proof for $\mathbf{n}\neq 0$ .

For $\mathbf{n}=0$ , the right-hand side of (4.7) equals

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}d\geqslant 1\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{c}\text{ primitive}\end{subarray}}\omega_{1}\biggl(\frac{|\mathbf{c}|d}{D}\biggr)\frac{1}{Q}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\geqslant 1\end{subarray}}\omega_{2}\biggl(\frac{q}{Q}\biggr)+O(D^{-A})=D^{2}+O(D^{-A}+Q^{-A}) $$

by Poisson summation and the normalizations (4.1). The desired result follows. ∎

## 5. Setup for proof of Theorem 2 in the balanced case

Let $X=X_{1}X_{2}$ . Until §12, we shall restrict ourselves to the balanced case

$$ X^{-\frac{1}{20}}\ll\frac{X_{1}}{X_{2}},\frac{X_{2}}{X_{1}}\ll X^{\frac{1}{20}}, $$

for the contents of §12 will imply the desired result otherwise with a remainder of $O(X^{2}\min(X_{1}/X_{2},X_{2}/X_{1}))$ (in light of the fact that $\eta=1/236$ , less than the saving in the exponent from §12 if (5.1) does not hold).

We begin with some reductions to simplify the notation for the remainder of the paper. By Fourier inversion, we have that

$$ \Phi^{\infty}(x_{1}^{\infty},x_{2}^{\infty})=\int_{K_{\infty}^{2}}\widehat{\Phi^{\infty}}(y_{1}^{\infty},y_{2}^{\infty})\psi(-x_{1}^{\infty}y_{1}^{\infty}-x_{2}^{\infty}y_{2}^{\infty})\,dy_{1}^{\infty}\,dy_{2}^{\infty}. $$

The decay of $\widehat{\Phi^{\infty}}$ implied by the derivative bounds of $\Phi^{\infty}$ implies that we may suppose (at an acceptable cost absorbed into the $\Omega^{O(1)}$ factor in the final remainder term) that $\Phi^{\infty}(x_{1}^{\infty},x_{2}^{\infty})=\phi_{1}(x_{1}^{\infty})\phi_{2}(x_{2}^{\infty})$ for some $\phi_{1},\phi_{2}\in C_{c}^{\infty}(K_{\infty}\setminus K_{\infty}^{0})$ upon performing a dyadic partition of unity on $\alpha_{1}$ , $\alpha_{2}$ .

We are therefore reduced to showing that

$$ \Sigma=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}\in\mathcal{O}_{K}\\
\boldsymbol{\ell}(\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2})=0\\
\alpha_{1}\equiv\beta_{1}^{\prime}(M)\\
\alpha_{2}\equiv\beta_{2}^{\prime}(M)\end{subarray}}\phi_{1}\biggl(\frac{\alpha_{1}}{X_{1}}\biggr)\phi_{2}\biggl(\frac{\alpha_{2}}{X_{2}}\biggr)=X^{2}\sigma_{\infty}\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\end{subarray}}\sigma_{p}+O((M\Omega)^{O(1)}X^{2-\eta}), $$

with

$$ \sigma_{\infty}=\int_{K_{\infty}^{2}}\phi_{1}(x_{1}^{\infty})\phi_{2}(x_{2}^{\infty})\delta(\boldsymbol{\ell}(x_{1}^{\infty}x_{2}^{\infty}))\,dx_{1}^{\infty}\,dx_{2}^{\infty}, $$

$$ \sigma_{p}=\int_{\mathcal{O}_{K,p}}\mathbbm{1}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\beta_{1}\equiv\beta_{1}^{\prime}\,(M)\\
\beta_{2}\equiv\beta_{2}^{\prime}\,(M)\end{subarray}}\delta(\boldsymbol{\ell}(\beta_{1}\beta_{2}))\,d\beta_{1}\,d\beta_{2}. $$

Our proof begins with an application of the 2-dimensional $\delta$ -method to detect the condition $\boldsymbol{\ell}=0$ , followed by an application of Poisson summation.

For the application of the $\delta$ -method, we fix two even $\omega_{1},\omega_{2}\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}\setminus{\left\{0\right\}})$ with

$$ 1=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\omega_{1}(|\mathbf{x}|)\,d\mathbf{x}=\frac{1}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\omega_{2}(x)\,dx. $$

These will remain fixed throughout the argument, with no dependence on any of the other parameters.

We now introduce a parameter $1\leqslant L\ll X^{\frac{1}{100}}$ (ultimately, it will be taken to be $X^{2\eta/3}$ ) and write

$$ D:=\frac{X^{\frac{1}{3}}}{L}. $$

Then, an application of the 2-dimensional $\delta$ -method (Theorem 4.1) and Poisson summation (Proposition 3.4) yields the following.

#### Proposition 5.1.

We have that

$$ \Sigma=-2\Sigma_{1}^{{\left\{\right\}}}+\Sigma_{2}^{{\left\{\right\}}}-2\Sigma_{1}^{{\left\{1,2\right\}}}+\Sigma_{2}^{{\left\{1,2\right\}}}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}j=1,2\end{subarray}}(-2\Sigma_{1}^{{\left\{j\right\}}}+\Sigma_{2}^{{\left\{j\right\}}}), $$

where for $S\subset{\left\{1,2\right\}}$ , we write

$$ \Sigma_{1}^{S}=\frac{X^{4}}{D^{2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\geqslant 1\\
M|q\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{q^{5}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}\\
\alpha_{i}=0\iff i\not\in S\end{subarray}}(S_{1}I_{1})(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2};q), $$

with

$$ S_{1}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2};q)=\frac{1}{q^{3}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\beta_{1},\beta_{2}\in\mathcal{O}_{K}/q\mathcal{O}_{K}\\
\boldsymbol{\ell}(\beta_{1}\beta_{2})\equiv 0(q/(q,M))\\
\beta_{1}\equiv\beta_{1}^{\prime}((q,M))\\
\beta_{2}\equiv\beta_{2}^{\prime}((q,M))\end{subarray}}\psi_{q}(\alpha_{1}\beta_{1}+\alpha_{2}\beta_{2}), $$

$$ I_{1}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2};q)=\int_{K_{\infty}^{2}}\omega_{1}\biggl(\frac{|\boldsymbol{\ell}(x_{1}^{\infty}x_{2}^{\infty})|MX}{qD}\biggr)\phi_{1}(x_{1}^{\infty})\phi_{2}(x_{2}^{\infty})\psi\biggl(-\frac{X_{1}x_{1}^{\infty}\alpha_{1}}{q}-\frac{X_{2}x_{2}^{\infty}\alpha_{2}}{q}\biggr)\,dx_{1}^{\infty}\,dx_{2}^{\infty}, $$

and

$$ \Sigma_{2}^{S}=\frac{X^{4}}{D^{2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}d\geqslant 1\\
\mathbf{c}\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}\\
(c_{1},c_{2})=1\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{d^{5}}\omega_{1}\biggl(\frac{|\mathbf{c}|d}{D}\biggr)\frac{d}{\sqrt{DX}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\geqslant 1\\
M|q\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{q^{5}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}\\
\alpha_{i}=0\iff i\not\in S\end{subarray}}(S_{2}I_{2})(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\mathbf{c};d,q), $$

with

$$ S_{2}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\mathbf{c};d,q)=\frac{1}{d^{3}q^{3}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\beta_{1},\beta_{2}\in\mathcal{O}_{K}/dq\mathcal{O}_{K}\\
\boldsymbol{\ell}(\beta_{1}\beta_{2})\equiv 0(d)\\
\det(\mathbf{c},\boldsymbol{\ell}(\beta_{1}\beta_{2}))\equiv 0(dq/(q,M))\\
\beta_{1}\equiv\beta_{1}^{\prime}((dq,M))\\
\beta_{2}\equiv\beta_{2}^{\prime}((dq,M))\end{subarray}}\psi_{dq}(\alpha_{1}\beta_{1}+\alpha_{2}\beta_{2}), $$

$$ I_{2}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2};\mathbf{c},d,q)=\int_{K_{\infty}^{2}}\biggl(\omega_{2}\biggl(\frac{dq}{M\sqrt{DX}}\biggr)-\omega_{2}\biggl(\frac{M\sqrt{X}\det(\mathbf{c},\boldsymbol{\ell}(x_{1}^{\infty}x_{2}^{\infty}))}{q\sqrt{D}}\biggr)\biggr)\phi_{1}(x_{1}^{\infty})\phi_{2}(x_{2}^{\infty})\\
\psi\biggl(-\frac{X_{1}x_{1}^{\infty}\alpha_{1}}{dq}-\frac{X_{2}x_{2}^{\infty}\alpha_{2}}{dq}\biggr)\,dx_{1}^{\infty}\,dx_{2}^{\infty}. $$

### 5.1. Proof of Theorem 2

In this subsection, we shall prove Theorem 2 assuming bounds we will show in §10 and §11 for $\Sigma_{1}^{S}$ and $\Sigma_{2}^{S}$ , respectively. The remainder of this paper will then be devoted to showing these bounds. We refer the reader to the next subsection, §5.2, for a explicit listing of the main propositions and what they bound, which may make the present subsection easier to read.

Putting together Propositions 10.6 and 11.6 to estimate $\Sigma_{1}^{{\left\{\right\}}},\Sigma_{2}^{{\left\{\right\}}}$ , we obtain that

$$ -2\Sigma_{1}^{{\left\{\right\}}}+\Sigma_{2}^{{\left\{\right\}}}=X^{2}\sigma_{\infty}\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\end{subarray}}\sigma_{p}+O\biggl((M\Omega)^{O(1)}X^{2+o(1)}\biggl(\frac{L^{4}}{X^{\frac{1}{3}}}+\frac{L^{2}}{X^{\frac{2}{3}}}\biggr)\biggr). $$

By Proposition 11.1, we have

$$ \Sigma_{2}^{{\left\{1,2\right\}}}\ll(M\Omega)^{O(1)}X^{2+o(1)}\biggl(\frac{1}{L^{\frac{3}{2}}}+\frac{L^{\frac{2}{7}}}{X^{\frac{2}{21}}}\biggr), $$

and by Proposition 10.1, we have that

$$ \Sigma_{1}^{{\left\{1,2\right\}}}\ll(M\Omega)^{O(1)}L^{47/8}X^{2-1/48+o(1)}. $$

At this point, we optimize to match the first two terms in (5.15) and (5.16), taking

$$ L=X^{\frac{2}{3}\eta} $$

with

$$ \eta=\frac{1}{236}=\frac{1/48}{3/2+47/8}\cdot\frac{3}{2}. $$

Putting this together with Propositions 10.4 and 11.3, which imply that

$$ \displaystyle\Sigma_{1}^{{\left\{j\right\}}} \displaystyle\ll\frac{X^{3+o(1)}}{DX_{2}^{2}}\ll X^{2-1/10+o(1)}, \displaystyle\Sigma_{2}^{{\left\{j\right\}}} \displaystyle\ll X^{2+o(1)}\frac{X^{\frac{3}{2}}}{X_{2}^{3}D}\ll X^{2-1/20+o(1)}, $$

yields that

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}j\leqslant 2\end{subarray}}(-2\Sigma_{1}^{{\left\{j\right\}}}+\Sigma_{2}^{{\left\{j\right\}}})-2\Sigma_{1}^{{\left\{1,2\right\}}}+\Sigma_{2}^{{\left\{1,2\right\}}}\ll(M\Omega)^{O(1)}X^{2-\eta+o(1)}. $$

from which Theorem 2 follows.

### 5.2. Structure of paper

The paper is organized as follows.

- §3 contains certain minor lemmas which will be used at various points throughout the proof, as well as the statement of Poisson summation we shall use. We also record in §3.4 all facts about the factorization of cubic Dedekind zeta functions and the bounds on the resulting $\GL_{2}$ Fourier coefficients.

- §4 contains a statement and proof of the two-dimensional delta method we use, providing a perturbation of the method of [LMV24] for our purposes.

- §6 contains estimates on $S_{1}$ that will be used to handle the nonzero frequencies $\Sigma_{1}^{{\left\{1,2\right\}}}$ as well as bounds pertaining to the zero frequency which will be used to bound $\Sigma_{1}^{{\left\{\right\}}}$ .

- §7 contains upper bounds on $S_{2}$ germane to the estimation of the nonzero frequency contribution $\Sigma_{2}^{{\left\{1,2\right\}}}$ , as well as a related estimate, Proposition 7.2, which will play a significant role in the estimation of the zero frequency $\Sigma_{2}^{{\left\{\right\}}}$ via §9.

- §8 contains upper bounds on both the oscillatory integrals and their derivatives which will be used to bound the nonzero frequency contributions $\Sigma_{j}^{{\left\{1,2\right\}}}$ .

- §9 contains preparatory lemmas leading up to the computation of the constants in front of the main terms of $\Sigma_{j}^{{\left\{\right\}}}$ and the secondary main term of $\Sigma_{1}^{{\left\{\right\}}}$ (which leads to the main term of Theorem 2)

### 5.3. Proof of Proposition 5.1

In this subsection, we carry out the application of the two dimensional delta method and the applications of Poisson summation that lead to the decomposition in Proposition 5.1. Recall that we are estimating

$$ \Sigma=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}\in\mathcal{O}_{K}\\
\boldsymbol{\ell}(\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2})=0\\
\alpha_{1}\equiv\beta_{1}^{\prime}\,(M)\\
\alpha_{2}\equiv\beta_{2}^{\prime}\,(M)\end{subarray}}\phi_{1}\biggl(\frac{\alpha_{1}}{X_{1}}\biggr)\phi_{2}\biggl(\frac{\alpha_{2}}{X_{2}}\biggr). $$

Applying Theorem 4.1 to decompose $\mathbbm{1}[\boldsymbol{\ell}(\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2})=0]$ (with $X$ , $D$ in Theorem 4.1 taken to be $X=X_{1}X_{2}$ , $D$ respectively, and any fixed choice of $\omega_{1}$ , $\omega_{2}$ with $\omega_{2}$ supported compactly away from $0$ ), we obtain that

$$ \Sigma=-2\Sigma_{1}+\Sigma_{2}, $$

where

$$ \Sigma_{1}=\frac{1}{D^{2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\geqslant 1\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}\in\mathcal{O}_{K}\\
\alpha_{1}\equiv\beta_{1}^{\prime}\,(M)\\

$$ \Sigma_{2}=\frac{1}{D^{2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}d\geqslant 1\\
\mathbf{c}\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}\\
(c_{1},c_{2})=1\end{subarray}}\omega_{1}\biggl(\frac{|\mathbf{c}|d}{D}\biggr)\frac{d}{\sqrt{DX}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\geqslant 1\end{subarray}}\\

Then, applying Poisson summation (Proposition 3.4) to both the sums over $\alpha_{1}$ , $\alpha_{2}$ yields that

The estimation of $S_{1}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2};q)$ reduces to the case of $q=p^{k}$ for $k\geqslant 1$ , for $S_{1}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2};q)$ is a multiplicative function in $q$ . These cases we resolve with the following collection of results.

For any $\alpha=n_{0}+n_{1}\zeta+n_{2}\zeta^{2}+n_{3}\zeta^{3}\in\mathcal{O}_{K}$ , we denote

$$ f_{\alpha}(x)=n_{3}x^{3}+n_{2}x^{2}+n_{1}x+n_{0} $$

and let $\Delta_{\alpha}=\mathrm{Disc}(f_{\alpha})$ .

The first is a result we will be applying in the general case

#### Proposition 6.1.

Suppose that $p$ is prime such that $p\nmid M$ . Then, we have that

$$ S_{1}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2};p)=a_{\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}}(p)+r_{\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}}(p) $$

where

$$ a_{\alpha}(p)=-1-\mathbbm{1}_{\begin{subarray}{c}p|\langle\alpha,1\rangle\end{subarray}}+\#{\left\{x(p):f_{\alpha}(x)\equiv 0(p)\right\}} $$

and $r_{\alpha}(p)$ satisfies

$$ r_{\alpha}(p)\ll\frac{1}{p}+\mathbbm{1}_{\begin{subarray}{c}p|N(\alpha)\end{subarray}}+p\mathbbm{1}_{\begin{subarray}{c}p^{2}|N(\alpha)\end{subarray}}+p^{3}\mathbbm{1}_{\begin{subarray}{c}p|\alpha\end{subarray}}. $$

In all other cases, we can afford to show the following upper bounds.

#### Proposition 6.2.

Suppose that $p$ is prime and $k\geqslant 1$ . Furthermore, suppose that $p^{s_{1}}||\alpha_{1}$ , $p^{s_{2}}||\alpha_{2}$ , $p^{s_{3}}||\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}p^{-s_{1}-s_{2}}$ . $$ S_{1}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2};p^{k})\ll(p^{k},M)^{8}kp^{3\min(s^{*},k)}(p^{k},\Delta_{\alpha^{\prime}})^{2/3}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}t\leqslant k-s^{*}\end{subarray}}p^{t}\mathbbm{1}_{p^{2t}|N(\alpha^{\prime})}. $$

At the zero frequency $\alpha_{1}=\alpha_{2}=0$ , we renormalize slightly, defining.

$$ \tilde{N}_{1}(q):=\frac{1}{q^{3}}S(0,0;q)=\frac{1}{q^{6}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\beta_{1},\beta_{2}\in\mathcal{O}_{K}/q\mathcal{O}_{K}\\

#### Proposition 6.3.

Let $p$ be a prime and $k\geqslant m_{p}$ . Then we have

## 7. Bounding $S_{2}$

Since we will choose the parameter $D$ in a way that shifts the burden of the trivial bound from $\Sigma_{2}$ onto $\Sigma_{1}$ , we require only an upper bound for $S_{2}$ for $\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}\neq 0$ . We shall show a somewhat less complete bound than we did in §6, opting to use the divisor bound from the sums over $d,q$ in §11.1 to yield the final bound on $\Sigma_{2}^{{\left\{1,2\right\}}}$ .

Recall the definition of $S_{2}$ in (5.12), that

$$ S_{2}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2};\mathbf{c},d,q)=\frac{1}{d^{3}q^{3}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\beta_{1},\beta_{2}\in\mathcal{O}_{K}/dq\mathcal{O}_{K}\\
\det(\mathbf{c},\boldsymbol{\ell}(\beta_{1}\beta_{2}))\equiv 0\,(dq/(q,M))\\
\boldsymbol{\ell}(\beta_{1}\beta_{2})\equiv 0\,(d)\\
\beta_{1}\equiv\beta_{1}^{\prime}\,((dq,M))\\
\beta_{2}\equiv\beta_{2}^{\prime}\,((dq,M))\end{subarray}}\psi_{dq}(\alpha_{1}\beta_{1}+\alpha_{2}\beta_{2}). $$

We begin by using orthogonality to detect $\beta_{i}\equiv\beta_{i}^{\prime}\,((dq,M))$ , which yields that

$$ S_{2}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2};\mathbf{c},d,q)=\frac{1}{(dq,M)^{8}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2}\,((dq,M))\end{subarray}}\psi_{(dq,M)}(-\gamma_{1}\beta_{1}^{\prime}-\gamma_{2}\beta_{2}^{\prime})S_{2}^{*}(\tilde{\alpha}_{1},\tilde{\alpha}_{2};\mathbf{c},d,q) $$

where

$$ S_{2}^{*}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2};\mathbf{c},d,q)=\frac{1}{d^{3}q^{3}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\beta_{1},\beta_{2}\in\mathcal{O}_{K}/dq\mathcal{O}_{K}\\
\det(\mathbf{c},\boldsymbol{\ell}(\beta_{1}\beta_{2}))\equiv 0\,(dq/(q,M))\\
\boldsymbol{\ell}(\beta_{1}\beta_{2})\equiv 0\,(d)\end{subarray}}\psi_{dq}(\alpha_{1}\beta_{1}+\alpha_{2}\beta_{2}), $$

with

$$ \tilde{\alpha}_{i}=\alpha_{i}+\frac{dq}{(dq,M)}\gamma_{i}. $$

As we do not care for losses of $M^{O(1)}$ , we will be fixing $\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2}$ from now on and just bounding $S_{2}^{*}$ . Write

$$ \gamma_{\mathbf{c}}(x,y,z;q):=(q,M)x(c_{2}-c_{1}\zeta)+q(y+z\zeta). $$

By orthogonality, we have

$$ \displaystyle S_{2}^{*}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2};\mathbf{c},d,q)= \displaystyle\ \frac{1}{d^{6}q^{4}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\,(dq)\\
y,z\,(d)\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\beta_{1},\beta_{2}\in\mathcal{O}_{K}/dq\mathcal{O}_{K}\end{subarray}}\psi_{dq}(\alpha_{1}\beta_{1}+\alpha_{2}\beta_{2}-\gamma_{\mathbf{c}}(x,y,z;q)\beta_{1}\beta_{2}) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\ \frac{1}{d^{2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\,(dq)\\
y,z\,(d)\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\beta_{1}\in\mathcal{O}_{K}/dq\mathcal{O}_{K}\\
\gamma_{\mathbf{c}}(x,y,z;q)\beta_{1}\equiv\alpha_{2}\,(dq)\end{subarray}}\psi_{dq}(\alpha_{1}\beta_{1}). $$

We shall show the following bound on $S_{2}^{*}$ .

#### Proposition 7.1.

We have that

$$ |S_{2}^{*}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2};\mathbf{c},d,q)|\\
\ll(dq)^{o(1)}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}g^{\prime}h^{\prime}|d\\
g^{\prime\prime}h^{\prime\prime}|q\\
g^{\prime}g^{\prime\prime}|\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}\\
(h^{\prime}h^{\prime\prime})^{2}|N(\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}/g)\end{subarray}}\frac{g^{4}h}{(dq)^{2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}x,y,z\,(dq)\\
g|\gamma_{\mathbf{c}}(x,y,z;q)\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}r|dq\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{r}\mathbbm{1}[Y_{\mathbf{c}}(\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2},x,y,z;q)\equiv 0\,(dq/r)], $$

where we write $g=g^{\prime}g^{\prime\prime},h=h^{\prime}h^{\prime\prime}$ and

$$ \displaystyle Y_{\mathbf{c}}(\alpha,x,y,z;q) \displaystyle=\langle\alpha,\gamma_{\mathbf{c}}(x,y,z;q)^{*}\rangle. $$

Here $\gamma^{*}=N(\gamma)/\gamma$ for $\gamma\in\mathcal{O}_{K}$ , so $Y_{\mathbf{c}}(\alpha,x,y,z;q)$ is a cubic form in $x,y,z$ . In particular, we have

$$ |S_{2}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2};\mathbf{c},d,q)|\\
\ll(dq)^{o(1)}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}g^{\prime}h^{\prime}|d\\
g^{\prime\prime}h^{\prime\prime}|q\\
g^{\prime}g^{\prime\prime}|M\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}\\
h^{\prime 2}h^{\prime\prime 2}|M^{2}N(\frac{\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}}{g^{\prime}g^{\prime\prime}})\end{subarray}}\frac{g^{4}h}{(dq)^{2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}x,y,z\,(dq)\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}r|dq\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{r}\mathbbm{1}[MY_{\mathbf{c}}(\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2},x,y,z;q)\equiv 0\,(dq/r)]. $$

As $S_{2}^{*}$ is multiplicative in $d,q$ , we may suppose throughout the proof that $q$ and $d$ are both powers of some prime $p$ .

Starting from (7.6), we scale and average over $(t,dq)=1$ and then apply orthogonality, in the same manner as in the proof of Proposition 6.1. This gives us

$$ S_{2}^{*}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2};\mathbf{c},d,q)=\frac{dq}{\varphi(dq)}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}r|dq\end{subarray}}\frac{\mu(r)}{(dq)^{2}r}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}x,y,z\,(dq)\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\beta_{1}\,(dq)\\

$$ \begin{cases}\langle\alpha_{1},\beta_{1}\rangle\equiv 0\,(dq/r)\\
\gamma_{\mathbf{c}}(x,y,z;q)\beta_{1}\equiv\alpha_{2}\,(dq)\end{cases}\implies\langle\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2},\gamma_{\mathbf{c}}(x,y,z;q)^{*}\rangle\equiv 0\,(dq/r). $$

with the notation $g=g^{\prime}g^{\prime\prime}$ and $h=h^{\prime}h^{\prime\prime}$ , as desired. ∎

For clarity, we renormalize at this point, taking

$$ \tilde{N}_{2}(\mathbf{c},d;q)=\frac{1}{d^{3}q^{4}}S_{2}(0,0;d,q)=\frac{1}{d^{6}q^{7}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\beta_{1},\beta_{2}\in\mathcal{O}_{K}/dq\mathcal{O}_{K}\\
\det(\mathbf{c},\boldsymbol{\ell}(\beta_{1}\beta_{2}))\equiv 0\,(dq/(q,M))\\
\boldsymbol{\ell}(\beta_{1}\beta_{2})\equiv 0\,(d)\\
\beta_{i}\equiv\beta_{i}^{\prime}\,((dq,M))\end{subarray}}1. $$

Notice that $\tilde{N}_{2}(\mathbf{c},d,q)$ is multiplicative in $d$ and $q$ . Recall the notation that we take $m_{p}=v_{p}(M)$ .

$$ \displaystyle D(\mathbf{c},p^{h};p^{k})\ll \displaystyle\ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}g=0\end{subarray}}^{h-m}\frac{h+k+1}{p^{4h+4k+4-6m}}\mathop{\mathop{\sideset{}{{}^{*}}{\sum}}}_{z\,(p^{h-m-g})}p^{h+k+1-m+\min\{\ell,k+g+1-m\}} \displaystyle\ll \displaystyle\ (h+k+1)p^{4m-2h-3k-3+\ell}. $$

Case 2: Suppose $p|c_{2}$ , then $(c_{1},p)=1$ as $(c_{1},c_{2})=1$ . Write $p^{b}||c_{2}$ for some $b\geqslant 1$ . Performing a change of variable $x\mapsto\overline{c_{1}}(x+p^{k+1-m}z)$ and $y\mapsto y-\overline{c_{1}}c_{2}z$ yields

$$ \displaystyle D(\mathbf{c},p^{h};p^{k})\ll \displaystyle\ \frac{1}{p^{4h+4k+4-2m}}\mathop{\mathop{\sideset{}{{}^{*}}{\sum}}}_{x\,(p^{h+k+1-m})}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}y\,(p^{h-m})\end{subarray}}N((\overline{c_{1}}c_{2}p^{m}x+p^{k+1}y-p^{m}x\zeta,p^{h+k+1-m})) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\ \frac{1}{p^{4h+4k+4-2m}}\mathop{\mathop{\sideset{}{{}^{*}}{\sum}}}_{x\,(p^{h+k+1-m})}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}y\,(p^{h-m})\end{subarray}}p^{4m}\ll p^{4m-2h-3k-3}. $$

Observe that (7.23), (7.26) and (7.30) are all smaller than (7.29). Hence (7.29) holds in all cases.

Finally, we have to show the bound for $\tilde{N}_{2}$ . Starting again from (7.17), with $\gamma$ completely determined by the other variables, we have

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{N}_{2}(\mathbf{c},p^{h};p^{m})\leqslant\frac{1}{p^{8m+5h}}\mathop{\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\,(p^{h+m})\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}y,z\,(p^{h})\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\beta\,(p^{h+m})\end{subarray}}}_{(x(c_{2}-c_{1}\zeta)+y+z\zeta)\beta\equiv 0\,(p^{h})}1=\frac{1}{p^{3m+5h}}\mathop{\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}x,y,z\,(p^{h})\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\beta\,(p^{h})\end{subarray}}}_{(x(c_{2}-c_{1}\zeta)+y+z\zeta)\beta\equiv 0\,(p^{h})}1. $$

Performing change of variables $y\mapsto y-c_{2}x$ and $z\mapsto z+c_{1}x$ gives us

$$ \tilde{N}_{2}(\mathbf{c},p^{h};p^{m})\leqslant\frac{1}{p^{3m+4h}}\mathop{\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}y,z\,(p^{h})\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\beta\,(p^{h})\end{subarray}}}_{(y+z\zeta)\beta\equiv 0\,(p^{h})}1=\frac{1}{p^{3m+4h}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}y,z\,(p^{h})\end{subarray}}N((y+z\zeta,p^{h})). $$

Pulling out the powers of $p$ from $y$ and $z$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{N}_{2}(\mathbf{c},p^{h};p^{m})\leqslant \displaystyle\ \frac{1}{p^{3m+4h}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}0\leqslant s,t\leqslant h\end{subarray}}\mathop{\mathop{\sideset{}{{}^{*}}{\sum}}}_{y\,(p^{h-s})}\mathop{\mathop{\sideset{}{{}^{*}}{\sum}}}_{z\,(p^{h-t})}N((p^{s}y+p^{t}z\zeta,p^{h})) \displaystyle\leqslant \displaystyle\ \frac{1}{p^{3m+4h}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}0\leqslant s,t\leqslant h\\
s\neq t\end{subarray}}p^{2h-s-t+4\min\{s,t\}}+\frac{1}{p^{3m+4h}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}0\leqslant s\leqslant h\end{subarray}}\mathop{\mathop{\sideset{}{{}^{*}}{\sum}}}_{y,z\,(p^{h-s})}p^{4s}N((y+z\zeta,p^{h-s})). $$

Note that

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{p^{3m+4h}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}0\leqslant s,t\leqslant h\\
s\neq t\end{subarray}}p^{2h-s-t+4\min\{s,t\}}\leqslant \displaystyle\ \frac{2}{p^{3m+2h}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}0\leqslant s<t\leqslant h\end{subarray}}p^{2s}\ll\frac{h+1}{p^{3m}}. $$

On the other hand, a change of variable $y\mapsto yz$ gives

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{p^{3m+4h}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}0\leqslant s\leqslant h\end{subarray}}p^{4s}\mathop{\mathop{\sideset{}{{}^{*}}{\sum}}}_{y,z\,(p^{h-s})}N(y+z\zeta,p^{h-s})\leqslant \displaystyle\ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}0\leqslant s\leqslant h\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{p^{3m+3h-3s}}\mathop{\mathop{\sideset{}{{}^{*}}{\sum}}}_{y\,(p^{h-s})}N(y+\zeta,p^{h-s}). $$

Lemma 3.3 gives us that this is $\ll(h+1)p^{-3m}$ . Hence we have the bound

$$ \tilde{N}_{2}(\mathbf{c},p^{h};p^{m})\ll\frac{h+1}{p^{3m}}. $$

Together with (7.29) which holds for all cases, we have for $k\geqslant m$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{N}_{2}(\mathbf{c},p^{h};p^{k})=\tilde{N}_{2}(\mathbf{c},p^{h};p^{m})+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}j=m\end{subarray}}^{k-1}D(\mathbf{c},p^{h};p^{j})\ll(h+k+1)p^{2m}. $$

This concludes the proof. ∎

## 8. Oscillatory integral estimation

In this section, we carry out the estimation of the oscillatory integrals $I_{1},I_{2}$ defined in (5.10), (5.13), respectively. Their treatments will be very similar to the applications of orthogonality that went into the treatments of the exponential sums $S_{1}$ , $S_{2}$ in §6, 7, though matters will be simpler in this archimedean analogue for we only seek an upper bound.

### 8.1. Estimation of $I_{1}$

The main result of this subsection is the following.

#### Proposition 8.1.

For any $A,k\geqslant 0$ , we have that

$$ q^{k}\frac{d^{k}}{dq^{k}}I_{1}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2};q)\ll_{A,k}|\tilde{\alpha}_{1}\tilde{\alpha}_{2}|_{\sup}^{-\frac{5}{6}}\,T^{-13/3+o(1)}\biggl(1+|\tilde{\alpha}_{1}|_{\sup}+|\tilde{\alpha}_{2}|_{\sup}\biggr)^{-A}, $$

where we write

$$ \tilde{\alpha}_{i}=\frac{\alpha_{i}DX_{i}}{MX}\quad\text{ and }\quad T=\frac{MX}{qD}. $$

#### Proof.

Differentiating under the integral, it is sufficient to bound, for any $\omega^{*}\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2}\setminus{\left\{0\right\}})$ and $\Phi_{1},\Phi_{2}\in C_{c}^{\infty}(K_{\infty}\setminus{\left\{0\right\}})$ , the integral

$$ I_{T}(\omega^{*},\Phi_{1},\Phi_{2}):=\int_{K_{\infty}^{2}}\omega^{*}(T\boldsymbol{\ell}(x_{1}^{\infty}x_{2}^{\infty}))\Phi_{1}(x_{1}^{\infty})\Phi_{2}(x_{2}^{\infty})e(-T(\langle x_{1}^{\infty},\tilde{\alpha}_{1}\rangle+\langle x_{2}^{\infty},\tilde{\alpha}_{2}\rangle))\,dx_{1}^{\infty}\,dx_{2}^{\infty}. $$

Repeated integration by parts implies that

$$ I_{T}(\omega^{*},\Phi_{1},\Phi_{2})\ll(1+|\tilde{\alpha}_{1}|_{\sup}+|\tilde{\alpha}_{2}|_{\sup})^{-A}, $$

This immediately gives the statement if $T\ll X^{\varepsilon}$ . So we’ll suppose from now on that $T\gg X^{\varepsilon}$ and $|\tilde{\alpha}_{i}|_{\sup}\ll T^{o(1)}$ .

We shall suppose without loss of generality that $|\tilde{\alpha}_{1}|_{\sup}\leqslant|\tilde{\alpha}_{2}|_{\sup}$ . Recalling $\boldsymbol{\ell}(x_{\infty})=(\langle x_{\infty},1\rangle,\langle x_{\infty},\zeta\rangle)$ , Fourier inversion implies that (8.3) equals

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\widehat{\omega^{*}}(y_{1},y_{2})\int_{K_{\infty}^{2}}\Phi_{1}(x_{1}^{\infty})\Phi_{2}(x_{2}^{\infty})\\
\cdot e(-T(\langle x_{1}^{\infty},\tilde{\alpha}_{1}\rangle+\langle x_{2}^{\infty},\tilde{\alpha}_{2}\rangle-\langle x_{1}^{\infty}x_{2}^{\infty},y_{1}+y_{2}\zeta\rangle))\,dx_{1}^{\infty}\,dx_{2}^{\infty}\,dy_{1}\,dy_{2}\\
=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\widehat{\omega^{*}}(y_{1},y_{2})\int_{K_{\infty}}\Phi_{1}(x_{1}^{\infty})\widehat{\Phi}_{2}(T(\tilde{\alpha}_{2}-x_{1}^{\infty}(y_{1}+y_{2}\zeta)))e(-T\langle x_{1}^{\infty},\tilde{\alpha}_{1}\rangle)\,dx_{1}^{\infty}\,dy_{1}\,dy_{2}. $$

We suppose from now on that

$$ |\tilde{\alpha}_{2}|_{\sup}\gg\frac{1}{T^{1-2\varepsilon}}, $$

for otherwise the statement immediately holds with $|\tilde{\alpha}_{1}\tilde{\alpha}_{2}|_{\sup}\leqslant|\tilde{\alpha}_{1}|_{\sup}|\tilde{\alpha}_{2}|_{\sup}\ll T^{-2+4\varepsilon}$ . Let $\eta_{\infty}=T(\tilde{\alpha}_{2}-x_{1}^{\infty}(y_{1}+y_{2}\zeta))$ so that by the change of variables

$$ \,dx_{1}^{\infty}=\frac{\,d\eta_{\infty}}{T^{4}(y_{1}^{4}+y_{2}^{4})}, $$

we have that $I_{T}(\omega^{*},\Phi_{1},\Phi_{2})$ is equal to

$$ \frac{1}{T^{4}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\frac{\widehat{\omega^{*}}(y_{1},y_{2})}{y_{1}^{4}+y_{2}^{4}}\int_{K_{\infty}}\widehat{\Phi}_{2}(\eta_{\infty})\Phi_{1}\biggl(\frac{\tilde{\alpha}_{2}-\eta_{\infty}/T}{y_{1}+y_{2}\zeta}\biggr)e\bigg(-\bigg\langle\frac{T\tilde{\alpha}_{2}-\eta_{\infty}}{y_{1}+y_{2}\zeta},\tilde{\alpha}_{1}\bigg\rangle\bigg)\,d\eta_{\infty}\,dy_{1}\,dy_{2}. $$

The contribution of $|\eta_{\infty}|_{\sup}>T^{\varepsilon}$ is $\ll_{A}T^{-A}$ from the decay of $\widehat{\Phi}_{2}$ . Also, from the support of $\Phi_{1}$ and the fact that both embeddings of $y_{1}+y_{2}\zeta$ are $\asymp|y_{1}^{4}+y_{2}^{4}|^{1/4}\asymp|\mathbf{y}|$ in magnitude, we have that in the support of the integrand above with $|\eta_{\infty}|_{\sup}\leqslant T^{\varepsilon}$ and (8.6),

$$ 1\asymp\biggl|\frac{\tilde{\alpha}_{2}-\eta_{\infty}/T}{y_{1}+y_{2}\zeta}\biggr|_{\sup}\asymp\biggl|\frac{\tilde{\alpha}_{2}}{y_{1}+y_{2}\zeta}\biggr|_{\sup}\asymp\frac{|\tilde{\alpha}_{2}|_{\sup}}{|\mathbf{y}|}. $$

In particular, it suffices to bound for $|\eta_{\infty}|_{\sup}\leqslant T^{\varepsilon}$ , some function $\Psi:\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}\times K_{\infty}\to\mathbb{C}$ with fixed compact support, compactly supported away from $0$ on the third coordinate and any derivatives of order $j$ being $O_{j}(1)$ , and some $\tilde{\alpha}_{i}^{\prime}\,(=\tilde{\alpha}_{i}-\eta_{\infty}/T)$ satisfying

$$ |\tilde{\alpha}_{i}^{\prime}|_{\sup}\asymp|\tilde{\alpha}_{i}|_{\sup}\asymp|\tilde{\alpha}_{i}^{\prime}|_{\infty}^{\frac{1}{4}} $$

the quantity (after a change of variable $y_{i}\mapsto|\tilde{\alpha}_{2}^{\prime}|_{\sup}y_{i}$ )

$$ \frac{|\tilde{\alpha}_{2}^{\prime}|_{\sup}^{-2}}{T^{4}}\int_{|\mathbf{y}|\asymp 1}\Psi\biggl(y_{1},y_{2},\frac{\tilde{\alpha}_{2}^{\prime}/|\tilde{\alpha}_{2}^{\prime}|_{\sup}}{y_{1}+y_{2}\zeta}\biggr)e\biggl(-T|\tilde{\alpha}_{1}^{\prime}|_{\sup}\biggl\langle\frac{\tilde{\alpha}_{1}^{\prime}\tilde{\alpha}_{2}^{\prime}|\tilde{\alpha}_{1}^{\prime}|_{\sup}^{-1}|\tilde{\alpha}_{2}^{\prime}|_{\sup}^{-1}}{y_{1}+y_{2}\zeta},1\biggr\rangle\biggr)\,dy_{1}\,dy_{2}. $$

It now remains to execute the $y_{1},y_{2}$ integrals. Taking any fixed $\phi\in C_{c}^{\infty}((1,2))$ with

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}}\phi(t)\,dt=1, $$

applying a change of variables $(y_{1},y_{2})\to(y_{1}/t,y_{2}/t)$ , and integrating against $\phi(t)\,dt$ yields that (8.11) equals

$$ \frac{|\tilde{\alpha}_{2}^{\prime}|_{\sup}^{-2}}{T^{4}}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{\phi(t)}{t^{2}}\int_{|\mathbf{y}|\asymp 1}\Psi\biggl(y_{1}/t,y_{2}/t,t\frac{\tilde{\alpha}_{2}^{\prime}/|\tilde{\alpha}_{2}^{\prime}|_{\sup}}{y_{1}+y_{2}\zeta}\biggr)e\biggl(-Tt|\tilde{\alpha}_{1}^{\prime}|_{\sup}\biggl\langle\frac{\tilde{\alpha}_{i}^{\prime}\tilde{\alpha}_{2}^{\prime}|\tilde{\alpha}_{1}^{\prime}|_{\sup}^{-1}|\tilde{\alpha}_{2}^{\prime}|_{\sup}^{-1}}{y_{1}+y_{2}\zeta},1\biggr\rangle\biggr)\,dy_{1}\,dy_{2}\,dt. $$

Executing the $t$ -integral and noting the decay of the Fourier transform in $t$ along with a change of variable $y_{2}\mapsto-y_{2}$ reduces us to bounding

$$ \frac{|\tilde{\alpha}_{2}|_{\sup}^{-2}}{T^{4}}\int_{|\mathbf{y}|\asymp 1}\mathbbm{1}\biggl[u_{0}y_{2}^{3}+u_{1}y_{1}y_{2}^{2}+u_{2}y_{1}^{2}y_{2}+u_{3}y_{1}^{3}\leqslant|\tilde{\alpha}_{1}^{\prime}|_{\sup}\frac{T^{\varepsilon}}{T}\biggr]\,dy_{1}\,dy_{2} $$

where we write

$$ \frac{\tilde{\alpha}_{1}^{\prime}\tilde{\alpha}_{2}^{\prime}}{|\tilde{\alpha}_{1}^{\prime}|_{\sup}|\tilde{\alpha}_{2}^{\prime}|_{\sup}}=u_{0}+u_{1}\zeta+u_{2}\zeta^{2}+u_{3}\zeta^{3}. $$

The bounds (8.10) imply that $\max_{0\leqslant i\leqslant 3}(|u_{i}|)\gg 1$ and so we obtain that (8.14) is

$$ \ll\frac{1}{T^{4}}|\tilde{\alpha}_{2}^{\prime}|_{\sup}^{-2}|\tilde{\alpha}_{1}^{\prime}|_{\sup}^{\frac{1}{3}}\,T^{-\frac{1}{3}+\frac{\varepsilon}{3}}\ll\frac{1}{T^{5}}|\tilde{\alpha}_{1}\tilde{\alpha}_{2}|_{\sup}^{-\frac{5}{6}}\,T^{\frac{2}{3}+\frac{\varepsilon}{3}}. $$

The desired result follows. ∎

### 8.2. Estimation of $I_{2}$

The estimate for $I_{2}$ we show is as follows.

#### Proposition 8.2.

For $|\mathbf{c}|d\asymp D$ , we have that $I_{2}=0$ unless $q\ll\sqrt{DX}/d$ , in which case we have the bound

$$ I_{2}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2};\mathbf{c},d,q)\ll_{A}|\tilde{\alpha}_{1}|_{\sup}^{-3/2}|\tilde{\alpha}_{2}|_{\sup}^{-3/2}T^{-4+o(1)}\biggl(1+|\tilde{\alpha}_{1}|_{\sup}+|\tilde{\alpha}_{2}|_{\sup}\biggr)^{-A}, $$

where

$$ T=\frac{M\sqrt{DX}}{dq}\quad\text{ and }\quad\tilde{\alpha}_{i}=\frac{\alpha_{i}X_{i}}{M\sqrt{DX}}. $$

#### Proof.

We have that

$$ I_{2}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2};\mathbf{c},d,q)=\omega_{2}\biggl(\frac{1}{T}\biggr)\hat{\phi}_{1}\biggl(T\tilde{\alpha}_{1}\biggr)\hat{\phi}_{2}\biggl(T\tilde{\alpha}_{2}\biggr)-I, $$

where

$$ I:=\int_{K_{\infty}^{2}}\omega_{2}(T\det(\tilde{\mathbf{c}},\boldsymbol{\ell}(x_{1}^{\infty}x_{2}^{\infty})))\phi_{1}(x_{1}^{\infty})\phi_{2}(x_{2}^{\infty})e(-T(\langle x_{1}^{\infty},\tilde{\alpha}_{1}\rangle+\langle x_{2}^{\infty},\tilde{\alpha}_{2}\rangle))\,dx_{1}^{\infty}\,dx_{2}^{\infty}, $$

with the notation $\tilde{\mathbf{c}}=\mathbf{c}d/D$ . The first term may be absorbed into the bound (8.17), so it remains to bound $I$ . Since $|\tilde{\mathbf{c}}|\asymp 1$ , repeated integration by parts gives us $I\ll(1+|\tilde{\alpha}_{1}|_{\sup}+|\tilde{\alpha}_{2}|_{\sup})^{-A}$ . We shall suppose from now on that $|\tilde{\alpha}_{i}|_{\sup}\ll X^{o(1)}$ .

As before, we begin with Fourier inversion. Noting that

$$ \det(\tilde{\mathbf{c}},\boldsymbol{\ell}(x_{1}^{\infty}x_{2}^{\infty}))=\langle\tilde{c}_{2}-\tilde{c}_{1}\zeta,x_{1}^{\infty}x_{2}^{\infty}\rangle, $$

we have

$$ I=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\widehat{\omega}_{2}(y)\int_{K_{\infty}^{2}}\phi_{1}(x_{1}^{\infty})\phi_{2}(x_{2}^{\infty})e(-T(\langle x_{1}^{\infty},\tilde{\alpha}_{1}\rangle+\langle x_{2}^{\infty},\tilde{\alpha}_{2}\rangle+\langle x_{1}^{\infty}x_{2}^{\infty},y(\tilde{c}_{2}-\tilde{c}_{1}\zeta)\rangle))\,dx_{1}^{\infty}\,dx_{2}^{\infty}\\
=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\widehat{\omega}_{2}(y)\int_{K_{\infty}}\phi_{1}(x_{1}^{\infty})\hat{\phi}_{2}(T(\tilde{\alpha}_{2}+y(\tilde{c}_{2}-\tilde{c}_{1}\zeta)x_{1}^{\infty}))e(-T\langle x_{1}^{\infty},\tilde{\alpha}_{1}\rangle)\,dx_{1}^{\infty}. $$

Similar to before, we make the change of variables

$$ \eta_{\infty}=T(\tilde{\alpha}_{2}+y(\tilde{c}_{2}-\tilde{c}_{1}\zeta)x_{1}^{\infty}) $$

so that

$$ I=\frac{1}{T^{4}(\tilde{c}_{1}^{4}+\tilde{c}_{2}^{4})}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{\widehat{\omega}_{2}(y)}{y^{4}}\int_{K_{\infty}}\phi_{1}\biggl(\frac{-\tilde{\alpha}_{2}+\eta_{\infty}/T}{y(\tilde{c}_{2}-\tilde{c}_{1}\zeta)}\biggr)\hat{\phi}_{2}(\eta_{\infty})e\biggl(-T\biggl\langle\frac{-\tilde{\alpha}_{2}+\eta_{\infty}/T}{y(\tilde{c}_{2}-\tilde{c}_{1}\zeta)},\tilde{\alpha}_{1}\biggr\rangle\biggr)\,d\eta_{\infty}\,dy. $$

As in the proof of Proposition 8.1, we may restrict to the case of $|\eta_{\infty}|_{\sup}<T^{\varepsilon},|\tilde{\alpha}_{2}|_{\sup}\gg T^{2\varepsilon-1}$ and fix an $\eta_{\infty}$ . Then, it is forced that $|y|\asymp|\tilde{\alpha}_{2}|_{\sup}$ . A trivial bound then gives us

$$ I\ll(1+|\tilde{\alpha}_{1}|_{\sup}+|\tilde{\alpha}_{2}|_{\sup})^{-A}T^{-4+o(1)}|\tilde{\alpha}_{2}|_{\sup}^{-3}. $$

Noticing that the same bound holds with $\tilde{\alpha}_{1}$ by swapping the roles of $\alpha_{1}$ and $\alpha_{2}$ , the desired result follows.

∎

## 9. Local density estimates

In this section, we record a number of facts about local densities, their averages, and associated objects, which will be of use in the following two subsections when analyzing zero frequencies.

### 9.1. Singular series estimates

Write

$$ V_{q}={\left\{(\beta_{1},\beta_{2})\in(\mathcal{O}_{K}/q\mathcal{O}_{K})^{2}:\beta_{i}\equiv\beta_{i}^{\prime}\,(M)\text{ for }i=1,2\right\}}, $$

and for $d,q\geqslant 1$ , $\mathbf{c}=(c_{1},c_{2})\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}$ with $(c_{1},c_{2})=1$ , let

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{N}_{1}(q)=\frac{1}{q^{6}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(\beta_{1},\beta_{2})\in V_{q}\\
\boldsymbol{\ell}(\beta_{1}\beta_{2})\equiv 0\,(q/(q,M))\end{subarray}}1, \displaystyle\tilde{N}_{2}(\mathbf{c},d;q)=\frac{1}{d^{6}q^{7}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(\beta_{1},\beta_{2})\in V_{dq}\\
\det(\mathbf{c},\boldsymbol{\ell}(\beta_{1}\beta_{2}))\equiv 0\,(dq/(q,M))\\
\boldsymbol{\ell}(\beta_{1}\beta_{2})\equiv 0\,(d)\end{subarray}}1. $$

Define the associated Dirichlet series

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{1}(s)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\geqslant 1\\
M|q\end{subarray}}\frac{\tilde{N}_{1}(q)}{q^{s}}, \displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{2}(s;\mathbf{c},d)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\geqslant 1\\
M|q\end{subarray}}\frac{\tilde{N}_{2}(\mathbf{c},d;q)}{q^{s}}. $$

We also write $\mathcal{D}_{1}^{*}(s)=\mathcal{D}_{1}(s)/\zeta(s)$ , $\mathcal{D}_{2}^{*}(s;\mathbf{c},d)=\mathcal{D}_{2}(s;\mathbf{c},d)/\zeta(s)$ so that

$$ \mathcal{D}_{1}^{*}(s)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\geqslant 1\\
M|q\end{subarray}}\frac{N_{1}^{*}(q)}{q^{s}},\quad\text{ where }\quad N_{1}^{*}(q)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}b|q/M\end{subarray}}\mu(b)\tilde{N}_{1}(q/b) $$

and

$$ \mathcal{D}_{2}^{*}(s;\mathbf{c},d)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\geqslant 1\\
M|q\end{subarray}}\frac{N_{2}^{*}(\mathbf{c},d;q)}{q^{s}},\quad\text{ where}\quad N_{2}^{*}(\mathbf{c},d;q)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}b|q/M\end{subarray}}\mu(b)\tilde{N}_{2}(\mathbf{c},d;q/b). $$

The absolute convergence of $\mathcal{D}_{1}(s)$ , $\mathcal{D}_{2}(s;\mathbf{c},d)$ for $\Re(s)>1$ is clear. Further analytic properties of these two relevant to us are contained in the following two propositions.

#### Proposition 9.1.

We have that

$$ N_{1}^{*}(q)\ll\frac{M^{4}}{q^{2-o(1)}}. $$

In particular, we have that $\mathcal{D}_{1}^{*}(s)$ is absolutely convergent for $\Re(s)>-1$ so that $\mathcal{D}_{1}(s)$ has a meromorphic continuation to $\Re(s)>-1$ with

$$ \mathcal{D}_{1}^{*}(0)=M^{2}\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\end{subarray}}\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{1}{p^{6k}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\beta_{1},\beta_{2}\,(p^{k})\\
\boldsymbol{\ell}(\beta_{1}\beta_{2})\equiv 0\,(p^{k})\\
\beta_{i}\equiv\beta_{i}^{\prime}\,(p^{m_{p}})\end{subarray}}1=M^{2}\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\end{subarray}}\sigma_{p}. $$

Furthermore, for $\sigma>\sigma_{0}>-1$ , we have that $|\mathcal{D}_{1}^{*}(s)|\ll_{\sigma_{0}}1$ .

In the computation of the local densities, we will encounter the following p-adic integral,

$$ \displaystyle\sigma_{p}(\mathbf{c},d)= \displaystyle\ \int_{\mathcal{O}_{K,p}^{2}}\mathbbm{1}_{\begin{subarray}{c}(\beta_{1},\beta_{2})\in V_{p^{k}}\\
d|\boldsymbol{\ell}(\beta_{1}\beta_{2})\end{subarray}}\delta(\det(\mathbf{c},\boldsymbol{\ell}(\beta_{1}\beta_{2})))\,d\beta_{1}\,d\beta_{2} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\ \lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{p^{7k}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\beta_{1},\beta_{2}\in V_{p^{k}}\\
p^{k}|\det(\mathbf{c},\boldsymbol{\ell}(\beta_{1}\beta_{2}))\\
p^{d_{p}}|\boldsymbol{\ell}(\beta_{1}\beta_{2})\end{subarray}}1. $$

Here $d_{p}=v_{p}(d)$ .

#### Proposition 9.2.

For $\mathbf{c}$ primitive and $d\geqslant 1$ , $\mathcal{D}_{2}^{*}(s;\mathbf{c},d)$ has an analytic continuation to $\Re(s)>-2$ . Furthermore, for $\delta>0$ , all $\Re(s)>-2+\delta$ satisfy the bound

$$ \mathcal{D}_{2}^{*}(s;\mathbf{c},d)\ll_{\delta}(|\mathbf{c}|d)^{o(1)}M^{4}(c_{1}^{4}+c_{2}^{4},d). $$

Furthermore, we have that

$$ \mathcal{D}_{2}^{*}(0;\mathbf{c},d)=M\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\end{subarray}}\sigma_{p}(\mathbf{c},d). $$

#### Lemma 9.3.

We have

$$ \sigma_{p}(\mathbf{c},d)=\tau_{p}(\mathbf{c}d), $$

where

$$ \tau_{p}(\mathbf{v}):=\frac{1}{(v_{1},v_{2},p^{\infty})}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k\geqslant 0\end{subarray}}S_{p}(\mathbf{v};k) $$

for $\mathbf{v}=(v_{1},v_{2})\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}\setminus\{(0,0)\}$ , and

$$ S_{p}(\mathbf{v};k):=\frac{1}{p^{9k+8\max\{0,m_{p}-k\}}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\beta_{1},\beta_{2}\in V_{p^{k}}\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}w\,(p^{k})\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{a}\,(p^{k})\\
(a_{1},a_{2},p)=1\end{subarray}}e_{p^{k}}(\langle\boldsymbol{\ell}(\beta_{1}\beta_{2})-\mathbf{v}w,\mathbf{a}\rangle) $$

satisfies

$$ S_{p}(\mathbf{v};k)\ll(k+1)(v_{1}^{4}+v_{2}^{4},p^{k})p^{-3k}. $$

#### Proof of Proposition 9.1.

The absolute convergence follows immediately from the bound (9.6), which itself follows from Proposition 6.3.

Now, for the product of local factors, note that $\mathcal{D}_{1}^{*}(0)$ , due to the absolute convergence implied by (9.6), satisfies

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{1}^{*}(0)=\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\end{subarray}}\biggl(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k\geqslant v_{p}(M)\end{subarray}}N_{1}^{*}(p^{k})\biggr) \displaystyle=\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\end{subarray}}\lim_{k\to\infty}\tilde{N}_{1}(p^{k})=\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\end{subarray}}\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{1}{p^{6k}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\beta_{1},\beta_{2}(p^{k})\\
\boldsymbol{\ell}(\beta_{1}\beta_{2})\equiv 0(p^{k-v_{p}(M)})\end{subarray}}1 \displaystyle=M^{2}\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\end{subarray}}\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{1}{p^{6k}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\beta_{1},\beta_{2}(p^{k})\\
\boldsymbol{\ell}(\beta_{1}\beta_{2})\equiv 0(p^{k})\end{subarray}}1=M^{2}\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\end{subarray}}\sigma_{p}, $$

as desired. ∎

#### Proof of Proposition 9.2.

All of these straightforwardly follow from the bounds of Proposition 7.2, for (7.16) implies the absolute convergence of $\mathcal{D}_{2}^{*}(s;\mathbf{c},d)$ for $\Re(s)>-2$ . The bound (9.9) also follows from (7.16).

Finally, (9.10), that $\mathcal{D}_{2}^{*}(0;\mathbf{c},d)$ is a product of local densities, follows identically to the proof of (9.7). ∎

#### Proof of Lemma 9.3.

What follows can be naturally written in terms of $p$ -adic integrals, though we shall proceed equivalently by taking limits of counts in $V_{p^{k}}$ .

By the limit characterization of $\sigma_{p}(\mathbf{c},d)$ in (9.8), we can perform a shift of $k$ to $d_{p}+k$ to write

$$ \sigma_{p}(\mathbf{c},d)=\lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{p^{7(d_{p}+k)}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\beta_{1},\beta_{2}\in V_{p^{d_{p}+k}}\\
p^{d_{p}+k}|\det(\mathbf{c},\boldsymbol{\ell}(\beta_{1}\beta_{2}))\\

### 9.2. Archimedean local densities

We shall require the following integral computation in §11.3, and can be thought of as amounting roughly to an archimedean analogue of some of the content of Lemma 9.3.

#### Lemma 9.4.

For $\omega\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}_{>0})$ , $\Phi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(K_{\infty}^{2}\setminus{\left\{(0,0)\right\}})$ , we have that

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\omega(|\mathbf{v}|)\int_{K_{\infty}^{2}}\Phi(x_{1}^{\infty},x_{2}^{\infty})\delta(\langle\mathbf{v},\boldsymbol{\ell}(x_{1}^{\infty}x_{2}^{\infty})\rangle)\,dx_{1}^{\infty}\,dx_{2}^{\infty}\,d\mathbf{v}\\
=2\tilde{\omega}(1)\int_{K_{\infty}^{2}}\Phi(x_{1}^{\infty},x_{2}^{\infty})|\boldsymbol{\ell}(x_{1}^{\infty}x_{2}^{\infty})|^{-1}\,dx_{1}^{\infty}\,dx_{2}^{\infty}. $$

#### Proof.

It will be sufficient to show that for any $\mathbf{w}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}\setminus{\left\{(0,0)\right\}}$ , we have

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\omega(|\mathbf{v}|)\delta(\langle\mathbf{v},\mathbf{w}\rangle)\,d\mathbf{v}=2\tilde{\omega}(1)|\mathbf{w}|^{-1}. $$

First, note that this is invariant under the action of $\SO(2)$ , so we may suppose without loss of generality that $\mathbf{w}=(|w|,0)$ . Letting $u=(u_{1},u_{2})$ , we obtain that the LHS of (9.39) is

$$ |\mathbf{w}|^{-1}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\omega(|u|)\delta(u_{1})\,du=|w|^{-1}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\omega(u_{2})\,du_{2}=2\tilde{\omega}(1)|w|^{-1}, $$

as desired. ∎

At a couple points, in our computation of the zero frequencies in §10.3, §11.3, we will encounter the following Riesz-type integral.

#### Lemma 9.5.

Suppose that $w\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n})$ and that $F:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{m}$ is such that $0$ is a regular value of $F|_{\mathrm{supp}\,w}$ 33 3 For any $a$ in $\mathrm{supp}(w)$ such that $F(a)=0$ , the matrix $(\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{i}}F_{j}(x)|_{x=a})$ has full rank, here $F|_{\mathrm{supp}\,w}=(F_{j})_{j\leqslant m}$ .. Then, we have that the function $U(s)$ , defined for $\Re(s)>-m$ as

$$ U(s)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}w(x)|F(x)|^{s}\,dx, $$

has a meromorphic continuation to $\mathbb{C}$ with simple poles at $-m-2k$ for $k\geqslant 0$ . Furthermore, we have that

$$ \underset{s=-m-2k}{\res}U(s)=\frac{2\pi^{m/2}}{4^{k}k!\Gamma(m/2+k)}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}\Delta_{F}^{k}w(x)\delta(F(x))\,dx, $$

where $\Delta_{F}$ satisfies $\Delta_{F}(\phi\circ F)=(\Delta_{\mathbb{R}^{m}}\phi)\circ F$ . Furthermore, for any $k\geqslant 0$ , $-m-2k-2<\sigma_{1}<\sigma_{2}<-m-2k$ , and $\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}|x|\leqslant 1\end{subarray}}|F(x)|\leqslant 1$ , we have that $s$ with $\Re(s)\in[\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}]$ satisfy

$$ U(s)\ll_{\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}}1. $$

#### Proof.

If $m>n$ , the regularity condition implies that $F$ is nonzero on $\mathrm{supp}\,w$ from which the result follows trivially, so suppose $m\leqslant n$ from now on.

Let $K=\mathrm{supp}\,w$ , and let $Z=K\cap F^{-1}(0)$ . Because $0$ is a regular value of $F$ on $K$ , there exists a neighborhood $\Omega$ of $Z$ on which $dF$ is surjective at every point.

By compactness, there also exists a neighborhood $0\in V\subset\mathbb{R}^{m}$ such that $K\cap F^{-1}(V)\subset\Omega$ .

Now, take $\chi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{m})$ such that for some $\varepsilon>0$ , $\mathbbm{1}_{|\cdot|<\varepsilon}\leqslant\chi\leqslant\mathbbm{1}_{V}$ , and take $w_{0}=w\cdot(\chi\circ F)$ , $w_{1}=w-w_{0}$ ,

$$ U_{j}(s)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}w_{j}(x)|F(x)|^{s}\,dx. $$

We have that $|F|\gg 1$ on $\mathrm{supp}\,w_{1}$ , so $U_{1}$ is entire.

Now, since $dF$ is surjective on $\mathrm{supp}\,w_{0}$ , we have that

$$ U_{0}(s)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}w_{0}(x)|F(x)|^{s}\,dx=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{m}}|y|^{s}g(y)\,dy. $$

where $g(y)\,dy=F_{*}(w_{0}(x)\,dx)$ (with $y\in\mathbb{R}^{m}$ , $x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ ).

To proceed, note that

$$ U_{0}(s)=\int_{0}^{\infty}r^{s+m-1}A(r)\,dr $$

where

$$ A(r)=\int_{|y|=1}g(yr)\,dy. $$

We record that the surface area of the $(m-1)$ -sphere equals

$$ \int_{|y|=1}1\,dy=\frac{2\pi^{m/2}}{\Gamma(m/2)}. $$

Now, Taylor expanding the radial $A(r)$ , we have that

$$ A(r)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k\leqslant N\end{subarray}}\frac{2\pi^{m/2}}{4^{k}k!\Gamma(m/2+k)}\Delta^{k}g(0)r^{2k}+O(r^{2N+2}). $$

The desired result follows for $\sigma>-m-2N$ upon executing the integral (9.46), noting that

$$ \Delta^{k}g(0)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}\Delta_{F}^{k}w(x)\delta(F(x))\,dx $$

by repeated integration by parts. ∎
