### 10.2. Estimation of $\Sigma_{1}^{{\left\{1\right\}}},\Sigma_{1}^{{\left\{2\right\}}}$ : the partial zero frequencies

In this section, we estimate $\Sigma_{1}^{{\left\{1\right\}}},\Sigma_{1}^{{\left\{2\right\}}}$ . Precisely, we show

#### Proposition 10.4.

Suppose that $j\in{\left\{1,2\right\}}$ and that $q/X_{2}\gg X^{\varepsilon}$ . Then, we have that

$$ \Sigma_{1}^{{\left\{j\right\}}}\ll X^{2+o(1)}\frac{X}{DX_{j}^{2}}. $$

For the proof, we shall require a minor lemma on the number of $x,y(q)$ for which $(x+y\zeta,q)$ has large norm, with averaging over $q$ . Specifically, we show

#### Lemma 10.5.

For any $Q,B\geqslant 1$ , we have that

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}Q<q\leqslant 2Q\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}x,y(q)\\
N((x+y\zeta,q))>B\end{subarray}}1\ll\frac{Q^{3}}{\sqrt{B}}. $$

#### Proof.

We shall sum over $g=(x,y,q)$ and $\mathfrak{h}=(x/g+y\zeta/g,q/g)$ separately, noting that

$$ \#{\left\{x,y\,(q):g\mathfrak{h}|x+y\zeta\right\}}=\frac{q^{2}}{g^{2}N\mathfrak{h}}. $$

It follows that

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}Q<q\leqslant 2Q\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}x,y\,(q)\\
N((x+y\zeta,q))>B\end{subarray}}1\leqslant\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}g\geqslant 1\\
\mathfrak{h}\subset\mathcal{O}_{K}\\
g^{4}N\mathfrak{h}>B\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}Q<q\leqslant 2Q\\
gN\mathfrak{h}|q\end{subarray}}\frac{q^{2}}{gN\mathfrak{h}}\leqslant Q^{3}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}g\geqslant 1\\
\mathfrak{h}\subset\mathcal{O}_{K}\\
g^{4}N\mathfrak{h}>B\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{g^{3}(N\mathfrak{h})^{2}}\ll\frac{Q^{3}}{\sqrt{B}}, $$

as desired. ∎

Armed with this, we can now quickly prove Proposition 10.4.

#### Proof of Proposition 10.4.

Throughout the proof, fix $\varepsilon>0$ sufficiently small.

Without loss of generality, suppose that $j=2$ . When $M|q$ , by orthogonality, we have

$$ S_{1}(0,\alpha_{2};q)=\frac{1}{M^{8}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2}\in\mathcal{O}_{K}/(M)\end{subarray}}\psi_{M}(\beta_{1}^{\prime}\gamma_{1}+\beta_{2}^{\prime}\gamma_{2})\frac{1}{q}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}x,y(q)\end{subarray}}G_{M}(\alpha_{2},x,y,\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2};q), $$

$$ \Sigma_{1}^{{\left\{2\right\}}}(\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2})=\frac{X^{4}}{D^{2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}X_{2}X^{-\varepsilon}\leqslant q\ll X/D\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{q^{6}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}x,y(q)\\

+O_{\varepsilon}\biggl(M^{6}\frac{X^{3+O(\varepsilon)}}{DX_{2}^{2}}\biggr). $$

In what remains, we shall fix $x,y,x_{1}^{\infty},q$ for which $N(M(x+y\zeta,q))\leqslant M^{4}B_{q}$ , as is implied by the bounds we have put in thus far, and show a bound of $O(X^{-100})$ on

### 10.3. Estimation of $\Sigma_{1}^{{\left\{\right\}}}$ : the full-zero frequencies

We begin with the treatment of the full-zero frequencies $\Sigma_{1}^{{\left\{\right\}}}$ . The main result of this subsection is as follows.

#### Proposition 10.6.

We have

$$ \Sigma_{1}^{{\left\{\right\}}}=-\frac{1}{2}X^{2}\sigma_{\infty}\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\end{subarray}}\sigma_{p}+\frac{X^{3}}{D}M^{-1}\mathcal{D}_{1}^{*}(1)\tilde{\omega}_{1}(1)\int_{K_{\infty}^{2}}\phi_{1}(x_{1}^{\infty})\phi_{2}(x_{2}^{\infty})|\boldsymbol{\ell}(x_{1}^{\infty}x_{2}^{\infty})|^{-1}\,dx_{1}^{\infty}\,dx_{2}^{\infty}\\
+O(M^{6}DX^{1+o(1)}). $$

The remainder of this section is devoted to the proof of Proposition 10.6. We can open up the definition of $I_{1}$ from (5.8) so that

$$ \Sigma_{1}^{{\left\{\right\}}}=\frac{X^{4}}{D^{2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\geqslant 1\\
M|q\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{q^{5}}S_{1}(0,0;q)\int_{K_{\infty}^{2}}\phi_{1}(x_{1}^{\infty})\phi_{2}(x_{2}^{\infty})\omega_{1}\biggl(\frac{|\boldsymbol{\ell}(x_{1}^{\infty}x_{2}^{\infty})|MX}{qD}\biggr)\,dx_{1}^{\infty}\,dx_{2}^{\infty}. $$

By Mellin inversion, we have that

$$ \Sigma_{1}^{{\left\{\right\}}}=\frac{X^{4}}{D^{2}}\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{(3)}\mathcal{D}_{1}(s+2)\tilde{\omega}_{1}(-s)U_{1}(s)\biggl(\frac{MX}{D}\biggr)^{s}\,ds, $$

where for $\Re(s)>-2$ ,

All we shall require, coming from Lemma 9.5, is that $U_{1}(s)$ has a meromorphic continuation to $\Re(s)>-3$ , in which region it has a pole only at $s=-2$ with

$$ \underset{s=-2}{\res}U_{1}(s)=2\pi\int_{K_{\infty}^{2}}\phi_{1}(x_{1}^{\infty})\phi_{2}(x_{2}^{\infty})\delta(\boldsymbol{\ell}(x_{1}^{\infty}x_{2}^{\infty}))\,dx_{1}^{\infty}\,dx_{2}^{\infty}, $$

and that $|U_{1}(s)|\ll|s+2|^{-1}$ for $\Re(s)>-3$ .

Therefore, applying Propositions 9.1 and moving the contour in (10.61) to $\Re(s)=-3+1/\log X$ yields that

$$ \Sigma_{1}^{{\left\{\right\}}}=\frac{X^{4}}{D^{2}}\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{(3)}\mathcal{D}_{1}(s+2)\tilde{\omega}_{1}(-s)U_{1}(s)\biggl(\frac{MX}{D}\biggr)^{s}\,ds\\

Recalling (9.7), (10.63), that $2\pi\tilde{\omega}_{1}(2)=1$ by (4.1), and that $\zeta(0)=-1/2$ , Proposition 10.6 follows from bounds on $U_{1}$ , $\zeta$ in vertical strips.

\langle\alpha,1\rangle=0\\
b|N(\alpha)\end{subarray}}1\ll b^{o(1)}\frac{Y^{3}}{b^{3/4}}. $$

### 11.3. Estimation of $\Sigma_{2}^{{\left\{\right\}}}$ : the full-zero frequencies

This is to cancel with the same illusory main term that arises in the evaluation of $\Sigma_{1}^{{\left\{\right\}}}$ along with the true main term. We show the following.

#### Proposition 11.6.

$$ \Sigma_{2}^{{\left\{\right\}}}=2\tilde{\omega}_{1}(1)\frac{X^{3}}{D}U_{1}(-1)M^{-1}\mathcal{D}_{1}^{*}(1)+O\left(\frac{X^{2+o(1)}}{D^{2}}+\frac{X^{3+o(1)}}{D^{4}}\right). $$

Our proof will amount to two maneuvers. The first is to show that $\Sigma_{2}^{{\left\{\right\}}}$ is a smooth sum over $\mathbb{Z}^{2}$ of a product of local densities. The second is to, with a good remainder term, estimate this smooth sum of a product of local densities by expanding the product into a convergent Dirichlet series whose coefficients are periodic and applying Poisson summation (as it will turn out, we do not have to truncate the Dirichlet series).

## 12. The unbalanced case

In this section, we shall quickly show the main theorem with a remainder of

$$ \ll M^{O(1)}X_{1}^{2}X_{2}^{2}\min\biggl(\frac{X_{1}}{X_{2}},\frac{X_{2}}{X_{1}}\biggr). $$

We will be brief and omit a number of details, for this result has already been shown implicitly in prior work (one way, for example, is to reverse the passage from Theorem 2 to Theorem 1, noting that both Daniel [Dan99] and Friedlander–Iwaniec [FI10, Theorem 22.20] deal with divisors in such an unbalanced range).

Assume without loss of generality that $X_{1}\geqslant X_{2}$ throughout this section, so we wish to show a remainder of $\ll M^{O(1)}X_{1}X_{2}^{3}$ . Throughout, we will ignore factors of $M^{O(1)}$ , absorbing them into implied constants without mention.

We will execute the sum over $\alpha_{1}$ first, which reduces to counting points of magnitude $\ll X_{1}$ in a codimension $2$ sublattice of $\mathbb{Z}^{4}$ . This codimension $2$ lattice has shortest vector of length $\ll|\alpha_{2}|_{\sup}$ , so Poisson summation or basic geometry of numbers estimates yields an accurate estimate for this inner sum over $\alpha_{1}$ . Executing the sum of these main terms over $\alpha_{2}$ then yields the desired result.

Write

$$ \Lambda(\alpha_{2})={\left\{\alpha_{1}\in\mathcal{O}_{K}:\boldsymbol{\ell}(\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2})=0\right\}}, $$

and let $\mathrm{covol}(\Lambda(\alpha_{2}))$ denote the covolume of $\Lambda$ in its $\mathbb{R}$ -span, a plane which we denote $W(\alpha_{2})\subset K_{\infty}$ .

We wish to estimate

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha_{2}\\
\alpha_{2}\equiv\beta_{2}^{\prime}(M)\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha_{1}\in\Lambda(\alpha_{2})\\
\alpha_{1}\equiv\beta_{1}^{\prime}(M)\end{subarray}}\Phi^{\infty}\biggl(\frac{\alpha_{1}}{X_{1}},\frac{\alpha_{2}}{X_{2}}\biggr). $$

Poisson summation in the $\alpha_{1}$ sum (or simply counting lattice points in a region, bounding the error based on the length of the boundary) yields that the inner sum equals

$$ \frac{X_{1}^{2}}{M^{2}\mathrm{covol}(\Lambda(\alpha_{2}))}\mathbbm{1}_{\boldsymbol{\ell}(\beta_{1}^{\prime}\alpha_{2})\equiv 0(M)}\int_{W(\alpha_{2})}\Phi^{\infty}\biggl(x_{1}^{\infty},\frac{\alpha_{2}}{X_{2}}\biggr)\,dx_{1}^{\infty}+O\biggl(\frac{X_{1}}{\sqrt{\mathrm{covol}(\Lambda(\alpha_{2}))}}\biggr). $$

We record that because of the support conditions on $\Phi^{\infty}$ , we have that

$$ |\alpha_{2}|_{\infty}\asymp|\alpha_{2}|_{\sup}\asymp X_{2} $$

for all terms that contribute to the above. Therefore, we have that $\mathrm{covol}(\Lambda(\alpha_{2}))\asymp|\alpha_{2}|_{\infty}^{2}\asymp X_{2}$ , so summing over $\alpha_{2}$ yields the desired remainder term and it remains to analyze the sum of main terms

$$ \frac{1}{X_{2}^{2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha_{2}\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{M^{2}}\mathbbm{1}_{\boldsymbol{\ell}(\beta_{1}^{\prime}\alpha_{2})\equiv 0(M)}\frac{1}{\mathrm{covol}(\Lambda(\alpha_{2}))}\int_{W(\alpha_{2})}\Phi^{\infty}\biggl(x_{1}^{\infty},\frac{\alpha_{2}}{X_{2}}\biggr)\,dx_{1}^{\infty}, $$

which we shall show equals $\sigma_{\infty}\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\end{subarray}}\sigma_{p}+O(1/X_{2}^{1-o(1)})$ .

By a change of variable in the $x_{1}^{\infty}$ integral and a closer analysis of the covolume, it can be checked that

$$ \frac{1}{M^{2}}\mathbbm{1}_{\boldsymbol{\ell}(\beta_{1}^{\prime}\alpha_{2})\equiv 0(M)}\frac{1}{\mathrm{covol}(\Lambda(\alpha_{2}))}\int_{W(\alpha_{2})}\Phi^{\infty}\biggl(x_{1}^{\infty},\frac{\alpha_{2}}{X_{2}}\biggr)\,dx_{1}^{\infty}=X_{2}^{-2}I_{\infty}\biggl(\frac{\alpha_{2}}{X_{2}}\biggr)\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\end{subarray}}I_{p}(\alpha_{2}), $$

where

$$ I_{p}(\alpha_{2}):=\int_{\mathcal{O}_{K,p}}\mathbbm{1}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\beta_{1}\equiv\beta_{1}^{\prime}(M)\\
\alpha_{2}\equiv\alpha_{2}^{\prime}(M)\end{subarray}}\delta(\boldsymbol{\ell}(\beta_{1}\alpha_{2}))\,d\beta_{1}, $$

$$ I_{\infty}(x_{2}^{\infty}):=\int_{K_{\infty}}\Phi^{\infty}(x_{1}^{\infty},x_{2}^{\infty})\delta(\boldsymbol{\ell}(x_{1}^{\infty}x_{2}^{\infty}))\,dx_{1}^{\infty} $$

are the expected local densities.

The desired result follows from Poisson summation in the $\alpha_{2}$ sum by expanding out the Euler product and applying Poisson summation (akin to §11.3.2) as follows.

At this point, we have reduced ourselves to showing

$$ \frac{1}{X_{2}^{4}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha_{2}\end{subarray}}I_{\infty}\biggl(\frac{\alpha_{2}}{X_{2}}\biggr)\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\end{subarray}}I_{p}(\alpha_{2})=\sigma_{\infty}\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\end{subarray}}\sigma_{p}+O(X_{2}^{-1+o(1)}). $$

Expanding the Euler product,

$$ \prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\end{subarray}}I_{p}(\alpha_{2})=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\geqslant 1\end{subarray}}N_{\alpha_{2}}^{*}(q), $$

with

$$ N^{*}(\alpha,q):=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}d|q\end{subarray}}\mu(d)\frac{d^{2}}{q^{2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\beta(q/d)\end{subarray}}\mathbbm{1}_{\boldsymbol{\ell}(\alpha\beta)\equiv 0(q/d)}. $$

It can be checked that

$$ \tilde{N}^{*}(\alpha,q)\ll q^{1+o(1)}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}d|q\end{subarray}}d\mathbbm{1}_{dq^{3}|N(\alpha)} $$

similarly (but in a simpler fashion) to the proofs of Propositions 6.3 and 7.2, so it follows that

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}|\alpha|_{\sup}\ll X_{2}\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q>Q\end{subarray}}N^{*}(\alpha,q)\ll\frac{X_{2}^{4}}{Q^{1-o(1)}}. $$

Therefore, taking $Q=X_{2}^{1-\varepsilon}$ , we may discard the contribution of $q>Q$ (if $\varepsilon\to 0$ ) for we have

$$ \frac{1}{X_{2}^{4}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha_{2}\end{subarray}}\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\end{subarray}}I_{p}(\alpha_{2})I_{\infty}\biggl(\frac{\alpha_{2}}{X_{2}}\biggr)=\frac{1}{X_{2}^{4}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha_{2}\end{subarray}}I_{\infty}\biggl(\frac{\alpha_{2}}{X_{2}}\biggr)\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\leqslant Q\end{subarray}}N^{*}(\alpha,q)+O(X_{2}^{-1+o(1)}). $$

It can be checked that $I_{\infty}$ is smooth (and that it is compactly supported is clear from the support of $\Phi^{\infty}$ ) and that $N^{*}(-,q)$ is $q$ -periodic, so it follows that

$$ \frac{1}{X_{2}^{4}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha_{2}\end{subarray}}I_{\infty}\biggl(\frac{\alpha_{2}}{X_{2}}\biggr)\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\leqslant Q\end{subarray}}N^{*}(\alpha,q)=\int_{K_{\infty}}I_{\infty}(x_{2}^{\infty})\,dx_{2}^{\infty}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\leqslant Q\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{q^{4}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\beta_{2}(q)\end{subarray}}N^{*}(\beta_{2},q)+O(X_{2}^{-A}). $$

The desired result follows upon noting that

$$ \sigma_{\infty}=\int_{K_{\infty}}I_{\infty}(x_{2}^{\infty})\,dx_{2}^{\infty}, $$

$$ N_{1}^{*}(q)=\frac{1}{q^{4}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\beta_{2}(q)\end{subarray}}N^{*}(\beta_{2},q), $$

recalling the bound $N_{1}^{*}(q)\ll q^{-2+o(1)}$ of Proposition 9.1 to reinsert the contribution of $q>Q$ , and recalling that

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\end{subarray}}N_{1}^{*}(q)=\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\end{subarray}}\sigma_{p}. $$

## 13. Proof of Theorem 1

In this section, we give a proof of Theorem 1.

It will actually follow relatively quickly from the more useful statement below, in whose proof we will carry out the passage from a sum over binary quartic form to a restricted sum over a quartic number field where we apply Theorem 2.

#### Theorem 13.1.

There exists $\delta>0$ such that for $Q,X\geqslant 1$ , $q_{0}\geqslant 1$ , $a_{0}\in\mathbb{Z}/q_{0}\mathbb{Z}$ , convex $\mathcal{R}\subset[0,1]^{2}$ with $\partial\mathcal{R}$ bounded and $0\not\in\mathcal{R}$ , we have

$$ \biggl|\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\leqslant Q\\
q\equiv a_{0}(q_{0})\end{subarray}}\biggl(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}m,n\in X\mathcal{R}\\
q|m^{4}+n^{4}\end{subarray}}1-\frac{\rho(q)}{q^{2}}X^{2}\vol\mathcal{R}\biggr)\biggr|\ll q_{0}^{O(1)}X^{2-\delta}\biggl(1+\biggl(\frac{Q}{X^{2}}\biggr)^{O(1)}\biggr), $$

where $\rho(q)=\#{\left\{x_{1},x_{2}\in\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}:x_{1}^{4}+x_{2}^{4}\equiv 0(q)\right\}}$ .

#### Proof of Theorem 1 assuming Theorem 13.1.

We have that

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n_{1},n_{2}\in\mathbb{Z}\\
0<n_{1}^{4}+n_{2}^{4}\leqslant N\end{subarray}}d(n_{1}^{4}+n_{2}^{4})=4\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n_{1},n_{2}\geqslant 1\\
n_{1}^{4}+n_{2}^{4}\leqslant N\end{subarray}}d(n_{1}^{4}+n_{2}^{4})+O(N^{1/4}). $$

Opening up the divisor function and summing over $d_{1}d_{2}=n_{1}^{4}+n_{2}^{4}$ , we obtain that the above equals

$$ 2\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}d_{1}\leqslant\sqrt{N}\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n_{1}^{4}+n_{2}^{4}\leqslant N\\
d_{1}|n_{1}^{4}+n_{2}^{4}\end{subarray}}1-2\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}d_{1}\leqslant\sqrt{N}\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n_{1}^{4}+n_{2}^{4}\leqslant d_{1}^{2}\\
d_{1}|n_{1}^{4}+n_{2}^{4}\end{subarray}}1. $$

By Theorem 13.1, this equals

$$ 2\kappa N^{1/2}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}d_{1}\leqslant\sqrt{N}\end{subarray}}\frac{\rho(d_{1})}{d_{1}^{2}}-2\kappa\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}d_{1}\leqslant\sqrt{N}\end{subarray}}\frac{\rho(d)}{d}+O(N^{1/2-\delta}) $$

the desired result follows upon noting that (see, e.g., [Dan99, §7])

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}d\leqslant D\end{subarray}}\frac{\rho(d)}{d^{2}}=c_{-1}\log D+c_{0}+O(D^{-{1/4}}), $$

and so by partial summation, we have that

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}d\leqslant D\end{subarray}}\frac{\rho(d)}{d}=c_{-1}D+O(D^{3/4}). $$

Collecting, the desired result follows. ∎

The remainder of this section is devoted to the proof of Theorem 13.1. We begin with some reductions. Existing level of distribution results for binary forms, namely [Dan99, Lemma 3.3], implies that

$$ \displaystyle\biggl|\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\leqslant Q\\
q\equiv a_{0}(q_{0})\end{subarray}}\biggl(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}m,n\in X\mathcal{R}\\
(m,n)\neq(0,0)\\
q|m^{4}+n^{4}\end{subarray}}1-\frac{\rho(q)}{q^{2}}X^{2}\vol\mathcal{R}\biggr)\biggr| \displaystyle\leqslant\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\leqslant Q\end{subarray}}\biggl|\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}m,n\in X\mathcal{R}\\
(m,n)\neq(0,0)\\
q|m^{4}+n^{4}\end{subarray}}1-\frac{\rho(q)}{q^{2}}X^{2}\vol\mathcal{R}\biggr| \displaystyle\ll(X\sqrt{Q}+Q)\log^{O(1)}X, $$

which is an acceptable $O(X^{2-1/200+o(1)})$ when $Q\leqslant X^{2-1/100}$ . Note too that we may suppose that $Q\leqslant X^{2+1/100}$ , for the contribution of $q\geqslant X^{2+1/100}$ is acceptable from the divisor bound by virtue of the term $(Q/X^{2})^{O(1)}$ .

Now, write

$$ R(Q,X;\Psi,W,a_{0},q_{0}):=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\equiv a_{0}(q_{0})\end{subarray}}\Psi\biggl(\frac{q}{Q}\biggr)\biggl(S_{q}(X;W)-M_{q}(X;W)\biggr), $$

where

$$ S_{q}=S_{q}(X;W):=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(m,n)\neq(0,0)\\
q|m^{4}+n^{4}\end{subarray}}W\biggl(\frac{m}{X},\frac{n}{X}\biggr), $$

$$ M_{q}=M_{q}(X;W):=\frac{\rho(q)}{q^{2}}X^{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}W(x,y)\,dx\,dy. $$

We now apply a dyadic partition of unity to the sum over $q$ . Fix some $\Psi\in C_{c}^{\infty}((3/2,5/2))$ satisfying

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k\in\mathbb{Z}\end{subarray}}\Psi\biggl(\frac{x}{2^{k}}\biggr)=1 $$

for all $x\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}$ . Then, we are reduced to showing that

$$ R(Q,X;\Psi,\mathbbm{1}_{\mathcal{R}},a_{0},q_{0})\ll q_{0}^{O(1)}X^{2-\delta} $$

for any scale $X^{2-1/100}\ll Q\ll X^{2+1/100}$ .

Now, fix some nonzero $\phi\in C_{c}^{\infty}((0,1)^{2})$ , write $\phi_{\Omega}(x)=\Omega^{2}\phi(\Omega x)$ , and let $W_{\mathcal{R}}=\mathbbm{1}_{\mathcal{R}_{1}}*\phi_{\Omega}$ , where

$$ \mathcal{R}_{1}={\left\{x\in\mathcal{R}:\mathrm{dist}(x,\partial\mathcal{R})>2/\Omega\right\}}. $$

Then, by a divisor bound, we have that

$$ R(Q,X;\Psi,\mathbbm{1}_{\mathcal{R}},a_{0},q_{0})=R(Q,X;\Psi,W_{\mathcal{R}},a_{0},q_{0})+O\biggl(\frac{X^{2+o(1)}}{\Omega}\biggr), $$

so Theorem 13.1 will actually follow from the following statement.

#### Proposition 13.2.

There exist $\delta>0$ with the following property. Let $X,\Omega,q_{0}\geqslant 1$ ,

$$ X^{2-1/100}\ll Q\ll X^{2+1/100}, $$

and let $W\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2}\setminus{\left\{0\right\}})$ satisfy

- (1) For all $x\in\mathrm{supp}(W)$ we have $\Omega^{-1}\ll|x|\ll\Omega$ .

- (2) For all $j_{1},j_{2}\geqslant 0$ , we have (13.15)

$$ \biggl\|\frac{\partial^{j_{1}+j_{2}}}{\partial x^{j_{1}}\partial y^{j_{2}}}W\biggr\|_{\infty}\ll_{j_{1},j_{2}}\Omega^{j_{1}+j_{2}}. $$

Then, we have that

$$ R(Q,X;\Psi,W,a_{0},q_{0})\ll(q_{0}\Omega)^{O(1)}X^{2-\delta}. $$

In the remainder of this section, we shall prove Proposition 13.2, beginning with preparation for the application of Theorem 2.

We start by analyzing the condition $q|m^{4}+n^{4}$ . If $(m,n)=1$ , we would have a correspondence ${\left\{q|m^{4}+n^{4}\right\}}\iff{\left\{\mathfrak{q}|m+n\zeta\right\}}$ , but we must deal with the possibility of primes that aren’t totally split dividing both $m$ and $n$ .

To this end, note that

$$ S_{q}(X;W)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}d\geqslant 1\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(m^{\prime},n^{\prime})=1\\
q|d^{4}(m^{\prime 4}+n^{\prime 4})\end{subarray}}W\biggl(\frac{dm^{\prime}}{X},\frac{dn^{\prime}}{X}\biggr)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}d\geqslant 1\\
r|d^{4},q\\
(r,q/r)=1\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(m^{\prime},n^{\prime})=1\\
q/r|m^{\prime 4}+n^{\prime 4}\end{subarray}}W\biggl(\frac{dm^{\prime}}{X},\frac{dn^{\prime}}{X}\biggr). $$

Letting $q/r=a_{1}$ , we obtain that

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\equiv a_{0}(q_{0})\end{subarray}}\Psi\biggl(\frac{q}{Q}\biggr)S_{q}(X;W)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}d\geqslant 1\\
r|d^{4}\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(m^{\prime},n^{\prime})=1\\
a_{1}|m^{\prime 4}+n^{\prime 4}\\
(a_{1},r)=1\end{subarray}}\Psi\biggl(\frac{a_{1}r}{Q}\biggr)W\biggl(\frac{dm^{\prime}}{X},\frac{dn^{\prime}}{X}\biggr). $$

We can discard the contribution of $d>D$ (to be specified, but it will be a small power of $X$ ultimately) at the cost of a remainder $O(X^{2+o(1)}/D)$ , so

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\equiv a_{0}(q_{0})\end{subarray}}\Psi\biggl(\frac{q}{Q}\biggr)S_{q}(X;W)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}d\leqslant D\\
r|d^{4},q\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(m^{\prime},n^{\prime})=1\\
a_{1}|m^{\prime 4}+n^{\prime 4}\\
(a_{1},r)=1\\
a_{1}r\equiv a_{0}(q_{0})\end{subarray}}\Psi\biggl(\frac{a_{1}r}{Q}\biggr)W\biggl(\frac{dm^{\prime}}{X},\frac{dn^{\prime}}{X}\biggr)+O\biggl(\frac{X^{2+o(1)}}{D}\biggr) $$

This sets up our passage to $K$ . There is a bijection

$$ \displaystyle{\left\{a_{1}|m^{\prime 4}+n^{\prime 4}\right\}} \displaystyle\leftrightarrow{\left\{\mathfrak{a}_{1}|(m^{\prime}+n^{\prime}\zeta)\right\}} $$

given by $N\mathfrak{a}_{1}\leftrightarrow\mathfrak{a}_{1}$ . Therefore, we have that

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\equiv a_{0}(q_{0})\end{subarray}}\Psi\biggl(\frac{q}{Q}\biggr)S_{q}\\
=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}d\leqslant D\\
r|d^{4}\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha^{\prime}\in\mathcal{O}_{K}\\
\boldsymbol{\ell}(\alpha^{\prime})=0\\
(\langle\alpha^{\prime},\zeta^{3}\rangle,\langle\alpha^{\prime},\zeta^{2}\rangle)=1\end{subarray}\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\begin{subarray}{c}\mathfrak{a}_{1}|(\alpha^{\prime})\\
(N\mathfrak{a}_{1},r)=1\\
rN\mathfrak{a}_{1}\equiv a_{0}(q_{0})\end{subarray}\end{subarray}}\Psi\biggl(\frac{rN\mathfrak{a}_{1}}{Q}\biggr)W\biggl(\frac{d\langle\alpha^{\prime},\zeta^{3}\rangle}{X},\frac{d\langle\alpha^{\prime},\zeta^{2}\rangle}{X}\biggr)+O\biggl(\frac{X^{2+o(1)}}{D}\biggr)\\
=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}d\leqslant D\\
r|d^{4}\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}h\geqslant 1\end{subarray}}\mu(h)\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha\in\mathcal{O}_{K}\\
\boldsymbol{\ell}(\alpha)=0\\
h|\alpha\end{subarray}\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\begin{subarray}{c}\mathfrak{a}_{1}|(\alpha)\\
(N\mathfrak{a}_{1},r)=1\\
rN\mathfrak{a}_{1}\equiv a_{0}(q_{0})\end{subarray}\end{subarray}}\Psi\biggl(\frac{rN\mathfrak{a}_{1}}{Q}\biggr)W\biggl(\frac{d\langle\alpha,\zeta^{3}\rangle}{X},\frac{d\langle\alpha,\zeta^{2}\rangle}{X}\biggr)+O\biggl(\frac{X^{2+o(1)}}{D}\biggr)\\
=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}dh\leqslant D\\
r|d^{4}\end{subarray}}\mu(h)\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha\in\mathcal{O}_{K}\\
\boldsymbol{\ell}(\alpha)=0\\
h|\alpha\end{subarray}\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\begin{subarray}{c}\mathfrak{a}_{1}|(\alpha)\\
(N\mathfrak{a}_{1},r)=1\\
rN\mathfrak{a}_{1}\equiv a_{0}(q_{0})\end{subarray}\end{subarray}}\Psi\biggl(\frac{rN\mathfrak{a}_{1}}{Q}\biggr)W\biggl(\frac{d\langle\alpha,\zeta^{3}\rangle}{X},\frac{d\langle\alpha,\zeta^{2}\rangle}{X}\biggr)+O\biggl(\frac{X^{2+o(1)}}{D}\biggr).\\
 $$

At this point, we wish to move from our sum over ideals to a sum over $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ . To do this, take $u:K_{\infty}^{\times}\to\mathbb{R}$ given by

$$ u(\alpha)=\log|\alpha|_{v_{1}}-\log|\alpha|_{v_{2}} $$

for the two complex places $v_{1},v_{2}$ of $K$ so that $u(\varepsilon_{0})\neq 0$ and pick any $\xi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R})$ such that

$$ \#\mu_{K}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k\in\mathbb{Z}\end{subarray}}\xi(t-u(\varepsilon_{0}^{k}))=\#\mu_{K}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k\in\mathbb{Z}\end{subarray}}\xi(t-ku(\varepsilon_{0}))=1 $$

for all $t\in\mathbb{R}$ . Taking $\Xi(x)=\xi(u(x))$ , we obtain that

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\varepsilon\in\mathcal{O}_{K}^{\times}\end{subarray}}\Xi(\varepsilon x)=1 $$

for all $x\in K_{\infty}^{\times}$ .

Applying this, we obtain that

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\equiv a_{0}(q_{0})\end{subarray}}\Psi\biggl(\frac{q}{Q}\biggr)S_{q}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}dh\leqslant D\\
r|d^{4}\end{subarray}}\mu(h)\Sigma_{d,h,r}(X;W)+O\biggl(\frac{X^{2+o(1)}}{D}\biggr), $$

where

$$ \Sigma_{d,h,r}(X;W)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}\in\mathcal{O}_{K}\\
\boldsymbol{\ell}(\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2})=0\end{subarray}}\Phi^{\infty}\biggl(\frac{\alpha_{1}}{X_{1}},\frac{\alpha_{2}}{X_{2}}\biggr)\Phi^{f}_{h,r}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}), $$

where $\Phi^{\infty}\in C_{c}^{\infty}(K_{\infty}^{2})$ , $\Phi^{f}_{h,r}:(\mathcal{O}_{K}/M\mathcal{O}_{K})^{2}\to\mathbb{C}$ are given by

$$ \Phi^{\infty}(x_{1}^{\infty},x_{2}^{\infty})=\Xi(x_{1}^{\infty})\Psi(N(x_{1}^{\infty}))W(\langle x_{1}^{\infty}x_{2}^{\infty},\zeta^{3}\rangle,\langle x_{1}^{\infty}x_{2}^{\infty},\zeta^{2}\rangle)\phi(|\boldsymbol{\ell}(x_{1}^{\infty}x_{2}^{\infty})|^{2}), $$

$$ \Phi^{f}_{h,r}(\beta_{1},\beta_{2})=\mathbbm{1}_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\beta_{1})r\equiv a_{0}(q_{0})\\
(\beta_{1},r)=1\\
h|\beta_{1}\beta_{2}\end{subarray}}, $$

where we write $X_{1}=X_{1}(r)=(Q/r)^{1/4}$ , $X_{2}(d,r)=(X/d)/X_{1}$ , $M=M(h,r)=hq_{0}r$ , and $\phi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R})$ is any fixed bump function with $\phi(0)=1$ .

It can be checked that the conditions of Theorem 2 hold with $M,\Omega,X_{1},X_{2},\boldsymbol{\ell}$ in the theorem as we have them here, $X$ taken to be $X/d$ . Therefore, we obtain that

$$ \Sigma_{d,h,r}=\frac{1}{d^{2}}X^{2}\sigma_{\infty}\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\end{subarray}}\sigma_{p}(h,r)+O\biggl((\Omega D)^{O(1)}X^{2-\eta+o(1)}\biggr), $$

where

$$ \displaystyle\sigma_{\infty} \displaystyle=\int_{K_{\infty}^{2}}\Phi^{\infty}(x_{1}^{\infty},x_{2}^{\infty})\delta(\boldsymbol{\ell}(x_{1}^{\infty}x_{2}^{\infty}))\,dx_{1}^{\infty}\,dx_{2}^{\infty}, \displaystyle\sigma_{p}(h,r) \displaystyle=\int_{\mathcal{O}_{K,p}^{2}}\Phi^{f}_{h,r}(x_{1}^{p},x_{2}^{p})\delta(\boldsymbol{\ell}(x_{1}^{p}x_{2}^{p}))\,dx_{1}^{p}\,dx_{2}^{p}. $$

We obtain that

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\end{subarray}}\Psi\biggl(\frac{q}{Q}\biggr)S_{q}(X;W)=X^{2}\sigma_{\infty}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}dh\leqslant D\\
r|d^{4}\end{subarray}}\frac{\mu(h)}{d^{2}}\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\end{subarray}}\sigma_{p}(h,r)+O\biggl(X^{2+o(1)}\biggl(\frac{1}{D}+\frac{(\Omega D)^{O(1)}}{X^{\eta}}\biggr)\biggr). $$

It remains to evaluate the sum of products of local factors, and show that it lines up with

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\end{subarray}}\Psi\biggl(\frac{q}{Q}\biggr)M_{q}(X;W). $$

We capture all our local computation in the following lemma, from which Theorem 13.1 follows upon taking $D$ a sufficiently small power of $X$ .

#### Lemma 13.3.

We have that

$$ \sigma_{\infty}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}dh\leqslant D\end{subarray}}\frac{\mu(h)}{d^{2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}r|d^{4}\end{subarray}}\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\end{subarray}}\sigma_{p}(h,r)=\biggl(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}W(x,y)\,dx\,dy\biggr)\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\equiv a_{0}(q_{0})\end{subarray}}\Psi\biggl(\frac{q}{Q}\biggr)\frac{\rho(q)}{q^{2}}+O\biggl(\frac{1}{D^{1-o(1)}}\biggr). $$

#### Proof.

First, note that with $Y=Q^{20}$ , we have

$$ \biggl(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}W(x,y)\,dx\,dy\biggr)\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\equiv a_{0}(q_{0})\end{subarray}}\Psi\biggl(\frac{q}{Q}\biggr)\frac{\rho(q)}{q^{2}}\\
=\frac{1}{Y^{2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\end{subarray}}\Psi\biggl(\frac{q}{Q}\biggr)\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}m,n\\
m^{4}+n^{4}\equiv 0(q)\end{subarray}}W\biggl(\frac{m}{Y},\frac{n}{Y}\biggr)+O\biggl(\frac{1}{Y^{2}}\biggr)\\
=\frac{1}{Y^{2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\end{subarray}}\Psi\biggl(\frac{q}{Q}\biggr)S_{q}(Y;W)+O\biggl(\frac{1}{Y^{2}}\biggr). $$

We may now perform the exact same maneuvers leading up to (13.24) (with the same choice of $D$ ) and apply Theorem 2 to yield the desired result. The error term follows from the rate of convergence of the RHS. ∎
